POLITICO https://www.politico.eu European Politics, Policy, Government News Mon, 16 Nov 2026 23:34:26 +0000 en hourly 60 https://wordpress.org/?v=6.9.11 French presidential rivals take aim at Le Pen in debate https://www.politico.eu/article/france-election-2027-presidential-candidates-target-marine-le-pen-tv-debate/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Mon, 16 Nov 2026 23:27:47 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=article&p=9336120 PARIS — Four French presidential hopefuls took aim at Marine Le Pen in a live televised debate on Monday, challenging the far-right leader on her plans for the economy, public housing and her combative relationship with progressive nonprofits.

The debate was centered around issues relating to the cost of living and saw candidates quizzed by voters struggling to make ends meet. Le Pen, who has a commanding lead in the polls, found herself on the receiving end of attacks from the other candidates on stage: far-left leader Jean-Luc Mélenchon, conservative leader Bruno Retailleau, the centrist Gabriel Attal and the center-left MEP Raphaël Glucksmann.

“Your budget trajectory is a joke, it doesn’t add up,” Retailleau said to Le Pen, referencing Le Pen’s promise to save €140 billion by 2032.

The most heated moment came when Le Pen detailed her plans to require charities that receive public money to refrain from meddling with politics.

“Your model is the same as that of your friends, Mr. Orbán and others, which is ultimately to shut up and stop those who do not think like you,” said Attal.

“You’ve got a list,” retorted Mélenchon, when Le Pen said she would deliver a list of charities she believed were too political.

Le Pen appeared to be playing it safe during the debate, trying to avoid being dragged into a damaging fight with her opponents. Her most pointed attacks targeted Attal, who is the leader of President Emmanuel Macron’s party Renaissance and was briefly prime minister in 2024.

“I don’t have any lessons to learn from someone who spent 10 years creating the biggest debt in the history of this country,” Le Pen said to Attal.

Le Pen and Mélenchon, who is polling in second place and could end up facing the far-right leader in the presidential runoff, avoided directly confronting each other during the debate.

Mélenchon instead took the opportunity to hammer home his proposal to impose a 100% tax on inheritances beyond €12 million.

“After 12 million, we take everything,” he said.

There were some lighter moments when Mélenchon and Le Pen both agreed the set was too cold. Retailleau chuckled when the far-left leader said the pensions system was not in crisis.

The center-right candidate Edouard Philippe, who is also the mayor of the port city of Le Havre, did not take part in the debate, as he had a conflict due to a municipal council meeting, according to his team. Philippe was once seen as the best-placed candidate to beat Le Pen in a runoff but has been struggling in the polls.

]]> en Brexit diminished us, Burnham says as he tees up closer EU ties https://www.politico.eu/article/andy-burnham-brexit-diminished-britain-pushes-closer-eu-ties-lord-mayors-speech/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Mon, 16 Nov 2026 22:48:21 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=article&p=9334842 LONDON — Andy Burnham laid out his case for reigniting the decade-old Brexit debate at an opulent London banquet Monday, claiming Britain lost more than it gained by leaving the EU.

Delivering his first major foreign policy speech at the Lord Mayor’s banquet in London, Burnham said he will sit down with EU leaders following Friday’s U.K.- EU reset summit — where the two sides are expected to sign an agri-food trade deal, link their emissions trading systems, and establish a new system of visas for young people— to work out “options for our long-term relationship.”

“This will take time, and we will present those options and our assessment of them to inform decisions in the next parliament. At every stage, the British people will be the boss”, Burnham said.

The U.K. prime minister set out his ambition to build a closer U.K. relationship with the EU at his first Labour conference as leader in September — confirming weeks later his desire for the U.K. to rejoin the EU within his lifetime.

“He will impale himself and his party on this point, and he needs to move off it because he won’t win — because the reality is that people are not fools,” Johnson said in an interview with the Telegraph newspaper published Monday.

Burnham acknowledged it would “be easier to say nothing about the EU,” but said the hard Brexit deal Britain struck with the bloc ended with “Britain eventually leaving on bad terms, with bad feeling.”

]]> en Concurrence : l’UEFA et une fédération de grands clubs de football européens visées par une plainte https://www.politico.eu/article/concurrence-luefa-et-une-federation-de-grands-clubs-de-football-europeens-vises-par-une-plainte/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Mon, 16 Nov 2026 18:30:50 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=pro-free&p=9332337 L’UEFA, l’instance dirigeante du football européen, et EFC, l’organisme représentant officiellement les clubs, ont fait l’objet lundi d’une plainte antitrust auprès de l’Union européenne déposée par une jeune organisation représentant des équipes qui ne sont pas dans l’élite.

L’Union des clubs européens (UEC, en anglais) a contesté un accord stipulant que l’UEFA reconnaît l’association Clubs de football européens (EFC, en anglais) comme “l’unique organisme” représentant les clubs du continent. Elle souhaite que la Commission européenne examine si cet accord exclusif enfreint les règles de l’UE relatives aux accords anticoncurrentiels et aux abus de position dominante.

L’UEC affirme que la représentation exclusive, combinée à ce qu’elle qualifie de “droits de vote inégaux” au sein d’EFC, permet aux clubs dominants d’influencer les règles qui s’appliquent à l’ensemble de la pyramide du football européen, aidant ainsi les grandes équipes, comme le Paris Saint-Germain ou le Bayern de Munich, à consolider leur avantage dans un secteur qui génère des dizaines de milliards d’euros de chiffre d’affaires annuel.

“La question est simple : qui a son mot à dire sur les règles qui déterminent l’avenir de chaque club ? Aujourd’hui, une seule organisation détient ce pouvoir pour l’ensemble des clubs européens, alors que la plupart d’entre eux n’y ont aucune influence réelle”, a pointé Dennis Gudasic, directeur exécutif du Lokomotiva Zagreb en Croatie et secrétaire général de l’UEC.

Reste qu’il sera difficile de convaincre Bruxelles d’ouvrir une enquête. La DG Concurrence, le puissant organe de la Commission chargé de l’application des règles de concurrence, s’est toujours montrée réticente à ouvrir des enquêtes dans les affaires liées au football, les considérant comme politiquement toxiques, selon des hauts responsables actuels et anciens de cette administration.

L’UEFA entretient également de bonnes relations avec la Commission. Son président Aleksander Čeferin et le commissaire européen chargé des Sports, Glenn Micallef, ont renouvelé un accord de coopération lors d’une réunion qui s’est tenue à Nyon, en Suisse, la semaine dernière.

En comparaison, les relations entre Bruxelles et la Fifa sont habituellement glaciales, selon trois responsables actuels et anciens de la Commission. Pourtant, Bruxelles s’est montré réticent à ouvrir une enquête officielle en matière de concurrence à l’encontre de l’instance dirigeante du football mondial au sujet de son calendrier des matchs internationaux, malgré la pression de députés européens.

“La mission de l’UEFA est de veiller au football européen dans son ensemble”, a déclaré l’instance dans un communiqué. “Nous l’accomplissons grâce à un modèle de gouvernance inclusif, qui associe toutes les parties prenantes : les fédérations nationales, les ligues, les clubs, les joueurs et les supporters ont tous voix au chapitre, et les décisions sont prises par le dialogue et le compromis. Dans le cadre de ce modèle de gouvernance, le memorandum of understanding UEFA-EFC, publiquement accessible, offre depuis 2008 un cadre stable et transparent pour la coopération avec les clubs à l’échelle européenne. Il garantit que les clubs participants prennent véritablement part à toutes les décisions concernant les compétitions européennes de clubs.”

Contactée par POLITICO, EFC n’a pas répondu à nos demandes de commentaire au moment de la parution de cet article.

Miguel Maduro, ancien avocat général à la Cour de justice de l’Union européenne et ancien président de la commission de gouvernance de la Fifa, a conseillé l’UEC dans le cadre de sa plainte. Pour ce détracteur régulier de la gouvernance actuelle du football européen et mondial, cette affaire vise “à utiliser le droit européen de la concurrence pour protéger le modèle sportif européen, caractérisé par des compétitions véritablement ouvertes et équilibrées”.

“Un système dans lequel un groupe restreint de clubs d’élite se voit conférer le pouvoir de décider qui peut participer aux compétitions européennes et comment les recettes sont réparties ne nuit pas seulement à la concurrence dans le football européen et national. Il détruit progressivement le modèle de compétition ouverte et équilibrée que l’UEFA elle-même prétend protéger”, a-t-il ajouté.

Qui parle au nom des clubs ?

L’UEC fonde en partie son argumentation sur l’arrêt rendu en 2023 par la Cour de justice de l’Union européenne concernant la Super Ligue. Elle fait valoir que les principes régissant la manière dont l’UEFA approuve les compétitions concurrentes devraient également s’appliquer à son accord avec EFC.

“Quiconque contrôle l’accès au football européen doit le faire selon des critères transparents, objectifs et non discriminatoires. Un accord qui impose aux clubs d’être représentés exclusivement par une association au sein de laquelle la plupart d’entre eux n’ont pas leur mot à dire, et qui exclut de ses rangs les clubs qui adhèrent à une autre association, ne répond pas à ces critères”, a déclaré Miguel Maduro.

Les règles d’EFC interdisent à ses membres d’adhérer à d’autres organisations transnationales représentant des clubs, à moins qu’elles ne soient reconnues par EFC ainsi que la Fifa ou l’UEFA. L’UEC fait valoir que les petits clubs n’ont pas d’influence significative au sein d’EFC, qui compte actuellement 920 membres dans le football masculin et féminin et est présidée par le puissant dirigeant qatari Nasser al-Khelaïfi. EFC indique sur son site web que tous ses membres peuvent élire des représentants au conseil d’administration et aux autres instances qui orientent ses travaux.

Lors de son lancement en avril 2023, l’UEC avait reçu le soutien de Margaritis Schinas, alors vice-président de la Commission européenne. “Je ne considère pas cela comme un problème ni comme un facteur de fragmentation”, avait-il déclaré à POLITICO lors de l’événement. “C’est une bonne chose.”

L’UEC affirme qu’un club a été averti en mai 2024 qu’il perdrait son statut de membre d’EFC s’il restait au sein de la nouvelle organisation. Et que 59 clubs auraient demandé que leur adhésion à l’UEC reste confidentielle, par crainte d’éventuelles pressions.

Sa plainte conteste également l’influence d’EFC sur la manière dont sont gérées des compétitions de l’UEFA. Selon l’UEC, EFC désigne 16 des 20 membres de la commission des compétitions interclubs de l’UEFA, chargée d’examiner les modifications apportées aux formats des tournois, aux modalités de qualification et aux rétributions financières. Elle estime que cela confère à un groupe restreint de clubs un pouvoir sur les règles qui concernent l’ensemble des clubs européens.

L’UEC fait valoir que les rétributions européennes renforcent l’avantage dont bénéficient déjà les clubs de haut niveau. Une étude citée dans son dossier d’information estime à 110 millions d’euros les recettes versées par l’UEFA à un club anglais au cours d’une seule saison, soit environ la moitié du chiffre d’affaires annuel total de certains de ses rivaux de la Premier League, selon les chiffres de 2023.

Cette étude, pour laquelle l’UEC a pris en charge une partie du travail sur les données, a également révélé qu’une cinquantaine de clubs se sont partagé environ 80% des places attribuées depuis 2000 en Ligue des champions, la compétition phare de l’UEFA. L’UEC a estimé que les mécanismes de gouvernance et de répartition des recettes contribuent à perpétuer cette tendance.

L’organisation souhaite que la Commission se procure et publie le memorandum of understanding actuel entre l’UEFA et EFC, et qu’elle ordonne la suppression de toute clause restrictive, ouvrant ainsi la voie à d’autres instances de clubs pour qu’elles soient reconnues et participent au processus décisionnel, tandis qu’EFC continue de représenter ses membres.

“Nous respectons pleinement le rôle de l’UEFA”, a déclaré le président de l’UEC, Ovidiu Costeșin, directeur général du CS Universitatea Craiova, champion de Roumanie en titre. “Mais le respect, ça ne peut pas vouloir dire le silence.”

“If people without the right of residence in the EU cannot be removed, our entire asylum system is made a mockery of. And we are not going to allow that,” Stocker said.

Stocker, Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen and government ministers from those two countries plus the Netherlands, Germany and Greece announced the plan at a press conference. The ministers stopped short of confirming they had cemented a deal, but said the hub would become operational during 2027.

There are still some “technical things” that have to be “sorted out,” Frederiksen said. “But the framework, the idea and the partnership is now in place.”

A reform of EU legislation adopted earlier this year made it possible for countries to negotiate deals to set up such deportation centers — as long as they comply with fundamental rights obligations.

The five countries plan to transfer people to Rwanda who have already gone through full asylum proceedings and were ordered to leave the EU.

The countries said they intend to target adults without children, and specifically people who don’t cooperate — or whose home countries don’t collaborate — in the deportation process. 

“For me, today marks a crucial step towards a new migration system; a system that safeguards the cohesion of our societies and answers the concerns of our citizens. To put it very short, it needs to be a democratic decision who can enter and who can stay in our societies,” Frederiksen said.

The five countries want to set up a reception center with the capacity to register and process 100 people at a time. Rejected asylum seekers who decide to stay in Rwanda rather than return to their country of origin would be given a residence permit and support to find a job and learn the language.

Rwanda’s Interior Minister Vincent Biruta said he expected few would opt to stay, but insisted that those who do “are not going to be kept in a camp … they’ll be integrated in our society.”

When sending migrants to Rwanda, their protection would remain a “key priority,” he said. The partnership would also have to meet the principle of non-refoulement, which forbids countries from forcing people to countries where they might be under threat, as well as other principles of international and European law, Berendsen added.

Rwanda has “considerable experience in hosting refugees” and a “strong track record of working with international organizations, including the International Organization for Migration (IOM) and the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees(UNHCR),” the Dutch minister said, adding that the five countries want to continue working with these organizations.

It’s not yet clear whether the IOM will be involved. In a statement Monday, the U.N. organization confirmed it had received a request from Rwanda to support EU return hub arrangements. “IOM has indicated that it can support in principle, provided its mandate and international standards can be upheld,” the organization said.

Civil society groups are not convinced.

In a joint reaction, 47 human rights, civil society and trade union groups warned that European authorities had previously reported “torture in detention, arbitrary arrests and impunity within the security services” in Rwanda, as well as a “real risk” of refoulement.

EU countries’ partnership “signals that Member States accept the risk of serious human rights violations against one of the most marginalized groups in society, in return for a deterrence goal that evidence clearly suggests they will not reach,” they wrote in a call on the EU to protect human rights. 

“I think we need to go beyond the existing cliché,” Biruta said on Monday. Rwanda is hosting more than 150,000 refugees “from as far as Afghanistan, from Sudan, Congolese, Burundians, and their rights were respected,” and it’s asking for a return hub system that meets “international law, European law and our national laws.”

“Looking at what we know from previous agreements with third countries, it has proven to be very difficult to guarantee any kind of human rights standard,” Meron Ameha Knikman, senior EU advocacy adviser at the International Rescue Committee, said ahead of the announcement. “It doesn’t matter what you put on paper — as long as it’s not under your jurisdiction, it’s extremely difficult if not impossible to enforce … any kind of guarantees.”

More hubs to follow

The ministers indicated that a deal with Rwanda could be the first in a string of return hub partnerships. “We are already exploring other partner countries, and I think other European countries will participate as well,” Frederiksen said.

Return hubs aren’t just about ramping up deportations, but also about sending a signal, she argued, adding that if people don’t assume they’ll get to stay after entering the EU irregularly, many would rethink their decision to attempt it. 

Frederiksen also pushed back against human rights concerns in the partnership with Rwanda.

“You have to remember that we are talking about people who don’t have a legal reason to be in Europe. It’s people who have entered illegally and that have no right to be protected in Europe or to stay,” Frederiksen said in a response to a question from POLITICO.

“What is the alternative? Is it to continue the system we have today?” she asked. “Because if you believe in human rights, I don’t like the current system. It’s broken. “If the prospect of dying in the desert, being raped and tortured in Libya, or drowning at sea doesn’t deter people, it’s hard to see how the possibility of being sent to Rwanda would dissuade people,” Judith Sunderland, senior associate director in the refugee and migrant rights division of Human Rights Watch, told POLITICO.

]]> en Europeans court China’s help to keep climate action on track https://www.politico.eu/article/europe-china-talks-ipcc-climate-reports/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Mon, 16 Nov 2026 16:33:43 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=pro&p=9332298 ANTALYA, Turkey — European governments will hold crunch talks with China this week, in a last-ditch bid to preserve the role of scientific advice in global climate summits. 

On the sidelines of the U.N. climate conference in Turkey’s Antalya, senior officials from several European delegations are meeting with their Chinese counterparts to get Beijing onside in a messy fight over scientific reports, five negotiators told POLITICO. 

“There’s a big diplomatic move,” said Francesco Corvaro, Italy’s climate envoy. “We’re working to create pressure.” 

The dispute ensnares the U.N.’s Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, a body which produces scientific assessments every five to seven years, and whose advice is considered the ultimate authority on the state of knowledge on global warming — and how to fight it. 

The IPCC’s scientists hope to release their next series of reports in 2028. But the timeline is set by consensus among world governments, and a small group of countries led by India and Saudi Arabia are seeking to postpone publication. 

As part of the dispute, they’re also blocking the body’s budget, throwing the IPCC into a funding crisis that could impede its work. 

Any delay to the next reports would deprive climate negotiators of fresh scientific input at the pivotal COP conference in 2028, when countries must assess their progress toward the Paris Agreement and take remedial action to fix shortfalls. (The exercise is known as the second global stocktake, or GST2).

“We have this issue with the IPCC — the alliance of Saudi Arabia and India that wants to postpone the reports,” said Corvaro. “Without the reports of the IPCC, it’s tough to have a good global stocktake. We need to know the details of how far we’re falling short if we want to respond.” 

European countries see China as key to resolving the impasse. If they manage to pull Beijing onside, the diplomats said, the blocking countries may fold. 

Finding time

The IPCC is due to publish three reports. The first will focus on the science, the second on how to prepare for the effects of climate change, and the third on how to ensure warming doesn’t get worse. The latter in particular is key for the global stocktake. 

Most countries want the body to deliver its reports in 2028, so that the stocktake at COP33 can draw on the latest scientific research. 

“It is essential that the IPCC continues its work and that the seventh assessment report can be delivered in good time to inform GST2,” EU chief negotiator Diana Acconcia told reporters last week. “Europe stands on the side of science.”

But India and Saudi Arabia want more time, arguing this will allow authors and governments from developing countries to review and approve the reports. 

“You have to give adequate time” to developing countries’ scientists, said an official from a developing country opposing the 2028 timeline. “It’s more of a principled position … not to stonewall or delay any studies.” The official spoke on condition his country not be identified. 

Countries pushing for the 2028 timeline — which include not only European governments but many developing countries highly vulnerable to climate change — disagree. 

“We have seen efforts to undermine the IPCC and to block its reports informing the next global stocktake,” said Marshall Islands President Hilda Heine last week. “Our Pacific scientists tell us the work can and should be completed on time.” 

The leaders of Norway and Brazil also backed the IPCC’s role in their speeches in Antalya last week. A French official told reporters that the Indian and Saudi Arabian efforts are “absolutely unacceptable because, in a way, it’s questioning science.” 

India and Saudi Arabia have suggested an alternate timeline that would deliver the first, science-only report in time for the stocktake — but push the other two, which focus on actions for countries to take, out to 2029. 

The process is highly political. The last stocktake, in 2023, produced a hard-fought decision signed by all governments to transition away from fossil fuels — the first time the need to do so was acknowledged in a conference decision. Saudi Arabia has since sought to walk back that outcome. 

This time, the timeline debate has also dragged in questions about IPCC funding, which is already under pressure due to the exit of the United States. Without a budget, the body’s work cannot continue. 

The result is a diplomatic deadlock over what used to be a technical detail. 

For six consecutive meetings, the IPCC’s assembly has failed to reach an agreement. Last month’s gathering in Ethiopia was suspended without result. Countries are due to meet again on Dec. 1. — the final chance to settle on a budget for the coming year.

“It’s not blocking,” the developing country official insisted. “A consensus has to be found. You can’t pass the budget in a non-transparent way.” 

India and Saudi Arabia also have the backing of Kenya and Russia, and diplomats say China has also objected to a fast publication timeline. But they believe that Beijing can be swayed. 

“China is in the middle — not completely aligned with Saudi Arabia and India,” said Corvaro. “We hope it’s possible to get a common understanding with them to underline the importance of science and data.” 

‘Everything is polarized’

As the Antalya summit brings together ministers from across the world, countries are hopeful the dispute could be resolved this week. But the stakes are high. 

“We have an opportunity here to get consensus on the IPCC with ministers here,” said one European diplomat, who was not authorized to speak on the record. “If they manage that, I can’t see next month’s IPCC meeting fail. Otherwise, it might be doomed.” 

Countries are mindful about not dragging the IPCC into a political debate at the COP — the two bodies fall under separate U.N. procedures — but say finding a resolution is a matter of urgency. 

“We have to be careful here. We don’t want to make things more difficult for the IPCC,” said a second European diplomat. “But if they don’t agree on a budget in December, it will delay and disrupt work on the next reports. That’s unacceptable.” 

The governments of India and Saudi Arabia did not respond to requests for comment. The developing country official said his country would oppose any attempt to address the IPCC issue in the Antalya summit’s decision text. 

A first draft of the final conference decision, released Monday, suggests countries note the “importance of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change for the global stocktake.” 

The IPCC, for its part, has welcomed government talks in Antalya. 

“I think governments talking here in this space [at COP] is extremely helpful,” said IPCC Vice Chair Diana Ürge-Vorsatz. “It’s crucial that we have a decision very soon, because it’s very difficult for the scientists involved, it’s difficult for the institution. It’s very difficult for everyone to be in this uncertainty.” 

The fact that the IPCC’s bureaucratic procedures had become so political was “difficult to watch,” she added. 

“Why has it become polarized? Because, unfortunately, at the moment everything is polarized. And because there are some parties that are trying to undermine what science is telling us, because they don’t want to do what it takes to address climate change,” said Acconcia, the EU negotiator. 

The bloc would strive for a resolution in Antalya, she added. “We will fight for this outcome to be there.”

]]> en Entwurf des COP-Abkommens sieht „sofortigen“ Ausstieg aus fossilen Brennstoffen vor https://www.politico.eu/article/entwurf-des-cop-abkommens-sieht-sofortigen-ausstieg-aus-fossilen-brennstoffen-vor/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Mon, 16 Nov 2026 15:35:04 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=pro&p=9332484 ANTALYA, Türkei — Australiens erster Entwurf für einen Abschlusstext der diesjährigen UN-Klimakonferenz soll als Gesprächsaufhänger dienen. Er sorgt jedenfalls dafür, dass die Diplomaten ins Gespräch kommen.

Die Australier, die den Vorsitz bei den Verhandlungen auf dem COP31-Gipfel in Antalya innehaben, haben am Montag einen 18-seitigen Entwurf für einen Beschlusstext vorgelegt. Dieser enthält eine Vielzahl klarer Positionen, darunter die Forderung nach einem „sofortigen“ Ausstieg aus fossilen Brennstoffen im Energiesektor.

Europäische Diplomaten, die sich bei POLITICO gemeldet haben, zeigen sich verwirrt über die Behauptung, der Text „erkenne“ die Forderung einiger Entwicklungsländer an, dass reiche Länder „bis 2030 Netto-Null-Emissionen erreichen“ sollten. Dieses Ziel liegt Jahrzehnte vor den Zielen der EU und des Vereinigten Königreichs zur Klimaneutralität im Jahr 2050.

Eine Verdreifachung der Finanzmittel für Entwicklungsländer zur Vorbereitung auf Klimakatastrophen auf 120 Milliarden Dollar pro Jahr wird auch für die Industrieländer, die mit Haushaltsengpässen im eigenen Land zu kämpfen haben, schwer zu verkraften sein.

Die Ölstaaten werden unterdessen aufgefordert, sich der Forderung nach einem schnelleren Ausstieg aus fossilen Brennstoffen anzuschließen, unter anderem „durch den sofortigen Umstieg weg von fossilen Brennstoffen in den Energiesystemen“.

„Zweifellos werden die Menschen ein wenig Zeit brauchen, um das zu verarbeiten … Es ist sehr umfassend“, sagte Chris Bowen, Australiens Klimaminister, gegenüber Reportern. „Und die heftigen Reaktionen, die es gegeben hat, sind genau so beabsichtigt. Damit wird eine Diskussion darüber angestoßen, wie der endgültige Entwurf aussehen wird, den wir den Vertragsparteien im Laufe der Woche vorlegen werden.“

Der Vorschlag der türkischen Mitveranstalter, ein freiwilliges globales Elektrifizierungsziel festzulegen – das laut Ankara am Samstag von rund 30 Ländern unterstützt wird –, wurde ebenfalls in den Beschlussentwurf aufgenommen. Mehrere Länder haben Einwände gegen die Idee neuer Ziele erhoben.

Jeder endgültige Beschluss der COP erfordert den Konsens aller Regierungen.

„Dieser erste Entwurf wird sich vom endgültigen Entwurf unterscheiden – genau dafür ist der Prozess ja gedacht“, sagte Bowen. „Ich gehe also davon aus, dass es bis Ende der Woche noch mindestens einen weiteren Entwurf geben wird, aber wir werden so lange weiterarbeiten, bis wir ein Dokument haben, auf das sich alle einigen können.“

EUobserver https://euobserver.com Independent EU journalism Mon, 16 Nov 2026 20:33:14 +0000 en-US hourly 1 https://wordpress.org/?v=7.1.4 ‘Emperor’s New Clothes’: Burnham breaks 10-year taboo on Brexit https://euobserver.com/249211/andy-burnham-brexit-and-the-obvious-truth/ Mon, 16 Nov 2026 19:00:00 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=249211 Boris Johnson's 'oven ready' Brexit deal never tasted very good. That's part of the 'obvious truth' about Brexit, according to UK PM Andy Burnham.]]> “It’s like the emperor’s new clothes – where no one is prepared to say the obvious truth. Well, I say it as I see it. And to be frank, the emperor has nothing on.” 

That’s the main salvo from UK premier Andy Burnham at a speech on EU-UK relations on Monday night (16 November) ahead of a summit in Brussels with EU leaders this Friday where he is expected to unveil a series of agreements ranging from food and carbon emissions, to youth mobility and industrial policy. 

“The Brexit we were given has not worked. We have lost more than we have gained,” he adds. 

It might seem remarkably uncontroversial from most Europeans on this side of the Channel, but saying it breaks a 10-year taboo among leaders of the UK’s main parties.  

Though the summit and accompanying deals are, in part, a PR exercise, they do mark the biggest step by far towards closer EU-UK ties since the 2016 referendum that took the Britain out of the bloc.

    ]]>         Europe’s mandate on Russia-Ukraine peace talks takes shape, as Putin escalates war https://euobserver.com/249307/eus-mandate-on-russia-ukraine-peace-talks-takes-shape-as-putin-escalates-war/ Mon, 16 Nov 2026 18:01:24 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=249307 While Europe crafts its role in the Ukraine peace talks, Vladimir Putin’s renewed offensive raises the cost of every EU decision.]]> Europe still doesn’t know how its so-called ‘Big 5’ will negotiate with Ukraine, the US, and Russia in practice, as Moscow escalates aggression on all fronts, while making “absurd” demands on Nato.

    Foreign ministers discussed the composition and mandate of the Big 5 format in Brussels on Monday (16 November).

    They spoke after the US and Russia invited Europe to join the peace process and EU leaders decided informally in Dublin last Friday that they should be represented by France, Germany, Italy, Poland, the UK, plus the EU institutions.

    And foreign ministers broadly endorsed the model.

    “The Europeans are determined to take charge of their own security and not let anyone write their history … for them,” said French foreign minister Jean-Noël Barrot on Monday.

    Germany’s Johann Wadephul said: “It is now clear who speaks [for Europe] … so let’s get to work”.

    “Poland will represent our entire region, the entire eastern flank … this means that we are in the game,” said Polish foreign minister Radek Sikorski.

    Danish foreign minister Lars Løkke Rasmussen also said: “I feel completely safe with this format”.

    But the Dublin accord still left open questions of the Big 5’s internal structure and who should represent the EU institutions.

    ]]>         Five EU countries tout Rwanda deportation partnership, but no formal deal as key details remain secret https://euobserver.com/249298/five-eu-countries-tout-rwanda-deportation-partnership-but-no-formal-deal-as-key-details-remain-secret/ Mon, 16 Nov 2026 17:50:37 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=249298 Rwanda is set to host a so-called EU return hub. No formal deal has been announced as technical details still need to be sorted out in negotiations. The hope is to start deporting people next year.]]> Rejected asylum seekers with deportation orders from possibly even as far away as Afghanistan may end up in Rwanda, following the announcement of talks spearheaded by five European countries with Kigali on Monday (16 November).

    No formal deal has been signed, posing questions on why Austria’s chancellor Christian Stocker and Denmark’s prime minister Mette Frederiksen, along ministers from Austria, Germany, Greece, the Netherlands and Rwanda’s interior minister Vincent Biruta, would announce anything.

    Instead, they gathered in Vienna, held a press conference and told journalists that a “partnership” had been agreed with Rwanda amid outstanding technical issues that still need to be sorted in the hopes of signing a formal deal in the coming months.

    Read more

    Rwanda revealed as EU’s first migrant return hub, but what’s in it for Kigali?

    The plan is to start deportations next year, said Austria’s Stocker despite Rwanda’s checkered human rights spanning political repression to its support of the M23 armed group operating in the eastern DR Congo.

    Even so Stocker described it as a “truly historic paradigm”, noting that Austria had deported more people than it has had asylum applications.

    His comments were largely echoed by Frederiksen, who said they now have a broad majority of European countries for a more sustainable migration policy.

    “We are now ready to move into more concrete steps,” said Frederiksen, who claimed they intend to remove incentives for “illegal migration” by sending a global signal that they are not welcomed in Europe.

    Little detail

    Nobody would cite potential costs when pressed on specifics.

    Rwanda’s Biruta said those received in Rwanda would have the opportunity to voluntarily continue home, go somewhere else, or integrate with legal residence and get jobs.

    He cited Rwanda’s experience of working with the International Organisation for Migration (IOM), a UN offshoot that flies in refugees stranded in Libya to a Rwandan hosted transit centre before being resettled elsewhere.

    “We are sensitive to people who are seeking asylum. This is our main motivation,” he said. “We are not looking at really getting money,” he said amid promises that people would not be put in camps.

    “We all care about human rights and freedom of expression, but human rights and freedoms of expression are not designed for robots,” French liberal MEP Nathalie Loiseau, chair of the parliament’s committee dealing with foreign interference, said during a hearing on the topic on Monday.

    Also on Monday, a report by Alliance4Europe revealed at least 8,505 Russian fake accounts were used ahead of the Swedish general elections in September. 

    They also found that public authorities tend to respond to disinformation targeting specific posts and campaigns, rather than account networks and systems spreading false narratives for months. 

    Read more

    Swedish election ‘not a priority’ for Moscow interference but still a target for troll farms and disinformation

    “[But] taking down single channels or posts achieves little while the infrastructure, the platform weaknesses and the payouts that sustain it stay in place,” reads the report.

    Russian propaganda networks switched from one country to another, changing profile names and photos to pose as local citizens. The researchers found that the same 550 fake accounts exposed ahead of the Dutch parliamentary elections in October 2025 then spread disinformation ahead of Hungary’s vote in April.

    While some spread false claims, often branded as coming from trusted news sources, many of them focus on following thousands of social media accounts with controversial and polarising lines, tricking the platform’s algorithm into boosting their reach, researchers said. 

    Read more

    EU sanctions needed against Russian bot and troll factories, MEPs say

    Though the impact of fakes is often not spectacular in size, electoral campaigns are “a moment of sensitivity” in which uncertainty plays a key role, Omri Preiss, from Alliance4Europe and one of the report authors, told EUobserver.

    ]]>         [Interview] ‘Georgia has reached final stage of autocratic consolidation,’ warns former deputy foreign minister https://euobserver.com/249198/interview-georgia-has-reached-final-stage-of-autocratic-consolidation-warns-former-deputy-foreign-minister/ Mon, 16 Nov 2026 16:54:43 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=249198 Georgia’s fall from EU frontrunner to near-total state capture is not just a regional tragedy but a case study in how Russia exploits European complacency to pull an entire country back into its orbit, explains former minister.]]> Georgia was once the frontrunner among countries aspiring to European Union integration. Twenty years ago, it was the only country in the region officially announcing its pro-European foreign policy course, declaring that Georgia wanted to become part of the EU and Nato, not only because of security guarantees, but because Europe had always been part of Georgia’s national identity and cultural belonging.

    This was demonstrated at length through those years with specific democratic reforms and the transformation of the country after the Rose Revolution in 2003.

    But since then, Georgia is now on a different path — one of illiberal democracy and pro-Russian sentiment.

    On 9 November, Guillaume Mercier, a European Commission spokesperson, announced that Georgia would not be invited to the Enlargement Forum happening this week (15-16 November).

    In an exclusive interview with the country’s former deputy foreign affairs minister Nino Kalandadze, we return to the biggest pivotal moments, as well as to how Georgia can be taken as a cautionary tale for the EU and its member states.

    “Georgia had previously been a failed state, but it was transformed almost overnight into a beacon of democracy,” Kalandadze told EUobserver.

    “There was a common understanding that democracy was a self-sustainable and self-sufficient project, and that all countries would eventually understand that democracy was what they needed to develop and thrive,” she says.

    Back in 2012, in the Transparency International ranking of its Corruption Perception Index, Georgia ranked ahead of several EU member states, including the Czech Republic, Latvia, Slovakia, Romania and Bulgaria.

    “We worked hard to eliminating organised crime and widespread corruption, topping international rankings, and becoming the number one reformer,” says Kalandadze.

    But in 2026, Georgia illustrates how unsustainable democratic achievements can become and how easily European integration can be reversed.

    Read more

    When the state turns on its own: Georgia’s civil society under siege

    Compared to where the country was 14 years ago, now “we have a ruling system that has remained in power for four consecutive years without majority support,” says Kalandadze.

    That is problematic, as it has banned international funding and civil society organisations, thereby “eliminating critical media and critical voices, establishing a system of political prisoners, with leaders and activists in prison or exile, and essentially cleared the way for itself by eliminating political competition,” Kalandadze says.

    And now, “we have essentially reached the final stage of autocratic consolidation,” says the former deputy foreign affair minister.

    “There is no way for us to maintain the instruments we need to move closer to European integration.”

    The soul is intact, the body is changing

    In 2024, some 20,000 Georgian citizens took to the streets to defend European integration, their freedom, and the choice they made about the foreign policy direction Tbilisi should follow. The demonstrators back then called it “March for Europe”.

    “This is still a freedom-loving and civilised society,” says Kalandadze. Indeed, “society made the effort to transform Georgia into a country that could obtain EU candidate status,” she also says.

    But the political system failed.

    “It is a combination of what many would call democratic naivety, but also perhaps convenience and ignorance on the part of international partners,” she says.

    The “blind eye” over Russia that the EU followed are one of the reasons for Kalandadze to explain Georgia’s U-turn.

    ]]>         What Marine Le Pen and Alice Weidel are planning for Brussels https://euobserver.com/248722/what-marine-le-pen-and-alice-weidel-are-planning-for-brussels/ Mon, 16 Nov 2026 14:52:23 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=248722 The AfD's Alice Weidel envisages reducing EU powers under existing rules within three years, pursuing treaty reform within seven, and using Germany's budgetary leverage along the way. Hot on her heels, Marine Le Pen is looking towards national elections across Europe to build a coalition of like-minded governments.]]> It’s been an early Christmas for Europe’s centre-left, watching even the most unshakeable populists stumble. Viktor Orbán’s defeat in April sent shockwaves through Europe after 16 years of entrenched cronyism, while Serbia followed hot on the heels of this October, reminding leaders that clinging to power is not the same as keeping the vote.

    And just when the drama seemed to subside, American voters, fed up with soaring prices, showed that the fury that lifts politicians to power can just as swiftly sweep them away.

    Should Brussels’ centre-left pop the champagne? Not so fast. The trouble with celebrating populists’ downfall is that the grievances that put them in office are still simmering.

    Alice Weidel in Germany and Marine Le Pen in France, for one, seem to have read the room. 

    ‘Frexit’ and the single currency

    Putting reform before withdrawal is no small thing. Le Pen has already ditched Frexit, while Weidel’s AfD is reconsidering its longstanding hostility to the euro.

    These are not merely plans to trim ‘Brussels bureaucracy’; they strike at the question of who gets the final say in Europe.

    For Germany’s export-dependent economy, leaving Europe’s single market and common currency could carry an uncomfortable price tag (€690bn).

    Rather, Weidel has baked into her proposed major reform of Germany’s role in the EU a shift from, in her words, its current paymaster role to one which reinforces German sovereignty.

    Weidel has even put a timetable on the ambition.

    Her party’s roadmap envisages reducing EU powers under existing rules within three years, pursuing treaty reform within seven, and using Germany’s budgetary leverage along the way. Hot on her heels, Le Pen is looking towards national elections across Europe to build a coalition of like-minded governments. 

    Both appear to recognise that power in Brussels can begin with power at home.

    And with populist parties gaining influence across the continent, changing the EU from within may offer more political leverage than another Brexit season.  

    Who holds the purse strings?

    The timing of Le Pen and Weidel’s rise could hardly be more uncomfortable. As the EU hammers out its nearly €2 trillion 2028–2034 budget, it is juggling the costly business of backing Ukraine, beefing up defence, and answering demands to spend more at home.

    For Le Pen and Weidel, Brussels’ budgetary nightmare could be the ideal stage to show who should really control the purse strings.

    Enter Le Pen, stage right.

    If in power following the 2027 French elections, Le Pen wants to slash France’s EU contributions while simultaneously demanding the return of €2.2bn annually in customs duties collected at French borders.

    Yet France is also a major beneficiary of EU agricultural funding.

    Cutting Brussels’ contributions could therefore raise awkward questions about who picks up the bill for French farmers. A September 2026 German Council on Foreign Relations study warns that a future French government could exploit the national ratification process to obstruct the EU’s revenue arrangements, even after a painstaking budget agreement. 

    Even if Brussels manages to hammer out a deal before French voters have their say, the squabble over who foots the bill is unlikely to vanish.

    The EU’s revenue rules still demand a chorus of unanimous approval and a round of national rubber-stamping, which could hand a future French government a fresh bargaining chip long after the ink dries on any spending pact.

    Brussels still faces the headache of actually securing the cash, with nationalist parties like AfD threatening to, if in power, block decisions until their demands are met. 

    Crowded calendar for 2027

    And Brussels has already spotted the storm. Emmanuel Macron has urged EU leaders to reach a budget agreement before the year is out, warning that Europe’s crowded 2027 election calendar could make negotiations considerably harder.

    But rushing through a deal does not guarantee it will put the matter to bed.

    Even after governments agree on spending, a future French administration could still challenge the arrangements for financing it. And while Weidel’s AfD remains outside Germany’s government, its proposed roadmap offers a glimpse of how the country’s financial weight might be used to demand wider institutional changes.

    The warning for Brussels is clear: the next Eurosceptic challenge may not come from those threatening to storm out, but from those determined to stay and rewrite the rulebook.

    Bomb threats, election interference, espionage, and sabotage. Cyberattacks are becoming an increasingly serious threat across Europe, affecting everything from public services to critical infrastructure. So, how prepared is Europe to deal with them?

    Let’s start with the scale of the threat. What’s been happening recently? Just last week, we’ve seen a wave of bomb threats across Europe. The latest target was Eurostar, which received a bomb threat on Thursday.

    Are we as vulnerable as it sometimes seems? Well, the EU has developed a number of tools to tackle cyber threats. But there are still some significant weaknesses.

    But in September, the European Court of Auditors published a rather critical assessment. It concluded that EU action only partially facilitates the detection of and response to major cybersecurity incidents.

    Information sharing is still limited, reporting procedures have weaknesses, and there are considerable delays in putting some of the mechanisms into operation.

    Even within a single country, several different authorities may be responsible for cybersecurity. So the challenge is to make sure they all follow compatible procedures and can communicate as smoothly as possible.

    Before coordinating anything, you need to focus on preventing attacks. Here the idea is to make systems as secure as possible, so that attacks can be prevented or their impact limited. This is an ongoing effort, at every level.

    The EU Agency for Cybersecurity, ENISA, plays an important role here. It provides guidance to public authorities and businesses, helps identify emerging threats and supports the development of more secure digital products and services.

    The EU has also introduced legislation to set minimum cybersecurity requirements. One of the main pieces of legislation is the NIS 2 Directive, which has been in force since October 2024.     But it also identified significant weaknesses in other areas, including healthcare, gas, maritime transport, public administration, space and information and communication technologies.

    But Jared Kushner, president Donald Trump’s envoy, says Washington is working on “a broader European security architecture” built on five goals: permanent security consultations, reliable crisis communications, greater military transparency, reciprocal measures to reduce escalation risks, and an enduring framework for long-term stability. 

    Russian foreign minister, Sergei Lavrov, agrees, calling for a wider European security arrangement before a deal to end the Ukraine war. 

    European capitals have been alarmed, and with reason.

    Read more

    Trump vows ‘beautiful’ Russia deal, as EU agonises over which envoy to send to Ukraine peace talks

    The future security of a continent is being discussed with a government that is still bombarding Ukrainian cities every night. European governments are trying to insert themselves into the talks and seemingly now have US backing.

    If a new order for Europe is being drawn up, Europeans should insist on writing into it the one word absent on Kushner’s list: nuclear.

    It is a striking omission, because every one of his five goals is at heart a nuclear question.

    Crisis communication, transparency and escalation risk matter so much precisely because this war is being fought – and  tensions with Moscow are increasing – in the shadow of the bomb.

    The gravest danger of the past five years has never been confined to the front line in Ukraine. It is that a nuclear-armed state has used the threat of mass destruction to try to keep others from coming to the aid of its victims.

    Since February 2022, president Vladimir Putin has used tacit and overt nuclear threats to try to achieve tactical advantage in the full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

    And now there are no guardrails. For almost a year, the United States and Russia have had no binding limits on their strategic arsenals.

    Who nuclear deterrence really rewards

    Defenders of nuclear deterrence say it keeps the peace.

    This war shows what it actually does. Russia felt emboldened by its nuclear arsenal to launch a full-scale invasion. Its nuclear weapons were not a shield against aggression. They were the arms holding the spear.

    Nuclear deterrence is a contest over who is more believably prepared to kill millions. A system that pays out to whoever appears most reckless is not a source of stability. It is an incentive to aggression. A path to disaster.

    This is why any settlement of this war matters far beyond Ukraine. If the terms of peace reward territory seized under nuclear coercion, the message will be heard by every would-be proliferator.

    Europe must not copy Moscow’s playbook

    Europe’s current response risks mirroring the logic it fears.

    In March, president Emmanuel Macron announced the first increase in France’s nuclear arsenal in more than three decades and launched a still undefined “forward deterrence” concept.

    Macron has also had himself photographed watching the test launch of a ballistic missile from a submarine accompanied with bellicose rhetoric, eliciting satirical comparisons with the North Korean leader Kim Jong Un.

    Read more

    Lithuania moves to lift ban on nuclear weapons as ‘Russians do not attack the strong’

    The fear behind these moves is understandable. But they accept Moscow’s rules of the game: a competition in conveying a credible threat of assured destruction that nobody wins, and in which the risk of miscalculation only grows.

    More nuclear weapons in more places is not a security architecture. It is a shorter fuse on the same bomb, and the continent seems willing to hand Vladimir Putin a match

    What Europe should put on the table

    If Washington wants to talk about European security, Europe should answer with concrete nuclear demands:

    First, declare nuclear threats inadmissible. In 2022, G20 leaders, following the lead of states that have joined the UN Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons, agreed that the use or threat of use of nuclear weapons is inadmissible. Any framework for European security should turn that principle into a binding commitment, with consequences for breaking it.

    Second, Europe can no longer host the nuclear chessboard of Russia and the US. Russian weapons in Belarus should be removed; as should the US weapons in six European countries.

    After that, interim verified limits to nuclear weapons must be agreed. Greater military transparency must mean warhead numbers and inspections, not just notifications of exercises. 

    Finally, the elimination of nuclear weapons must be anchored in law that already exists. The Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons, already signed or ratified by a global majority, bans not only the use and possession of nuclear weapons but also the threat to use them. 

    Read more

    Putin and the threat of a tactical nuclear attack

    In three weeks, countries meet at the UN for the treaty’s first review conference. European governments that want a security order resistant to blackmail should be in the room, at the very least as observers.

    Moscow and Washington cannot dictate Europe’s future. Neither should nuclear threats, whoever makes them. A peace that leaves the bomb as the final arbiter of borders is not a lasting peace. It is a pause before the next blackmail attempt.

    Estonian prime minister Kristen Michal has laid out how to build up Europe’s defences. He also urges the use of Russian assets frozen in Belgium, and discusses Baltic expertise in fighting Putin. The liberal leader spoke with Ondřej Kundra in early November.

    Has anything brought you satisfaction recently as a politician?

    Kristen Michal: I recently attended the opening of Estonia’s largest timber building in northern Estonia. It may sound amusing this would bring joy to a prime minister, but in my previous role as environment minister, I launched this project in 2023.

    It is a truly beautiful area, both in nature and culture – I recommend visiting. It has a maritime museum in a former seaplane harbour, as well as Estonia’s only submarine. And beside it stands the largest wooden building of its kind: our new natural history museum, under whose roof we want to bring together institutions focused on ecology and climate.

    It is not merely a wooden structure; it is also probably one of most cost-effective buildings, amounting to about €2,100 to €2,200 per square metre.

    One of our state agencies began its construction, and I was genuinely emotional at the opening ceremony – it is rewarding for a politician to see that something they started was actually completed.

    Estonia is one of the foresighted Baltic member states which has warned for years about the Russian threat. EU Commission president Ursula von der Leyen has recognised that Baltic warnings about Russian expansionism unfortunately came true…

    I would probably have been happier if Baltic states had not been right. We spoke about Russia in the past, warning that Putin had imperial dreams of restoring the Soviet Union, that he was not concerned solely with Ukrainian territory, but also with stripping Ukraine of its sovereignty, or that he had further territorial ambitions. It would of course have been preferable if our warnings had not been proven wrong. But they were proven right.

    Even before the full-scale invasion of Ukraine, you warned the West about energy dependence on Russia and about unpreparedness for cyber threats. Now, Europe has learned its lesson. Are you satisfied that EU member states have woken up to reality, or do you think they remain blind to such threats?

    This article continues, but the full version is available only to EUobserver.com subscribers. Visit account.euobserver.com/membership

    ]]>         ‘No added value’: MEPs to probe Africa’s flagship €5bn Lobito Corridor project in Global Gateway scrutiny https://euobserver.com/248791/no-added-value-meps-to-probe-africas-flagship-e5bn-lobito-corridor-project-in-global-gateway-scrutiny/ Fri, 13 Nov 2026 13:59:47 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=248791 MEPs will hold a scrutiny hearing on a €5bn African rail project that European Parliament development committee chair Barry Andrews says has "no value added."]]> MEPs will hold a scrutiny hearing in January on the EU’s Lobito Corridor project, the flagship scheme of the bloc’s Global Gateway programme, amid growing concerns about the value and governance of the scheme. 

    The project is supposed to connect the port of Lobito on Angola’s Atlantic Coast to the mineral-rich Katanga province in the Democratic Republic of Congo and the Copperbelt in Zambia. 

    The European Parliament’s development committee says that the hearing will look into whether the project is effective. 

    EU lawmakers have previously expressed concerns about the governance of Global Gateway, a plan to raise €300bn for infrastructure projects in developing countries that is widely seen as Europe’s response to China’s Belt and Road Initiative (BRI) and the EU’s own urgent need to secure access to critical minerals. 

    The EU Commission says that more than €2bn has already been raised by the EU for the Lobito Corridor project, part of a joint €5bn plan with the United States, as part of close to €150bn in projects across Africa. 

    Read more

    Biden says goodbye in Africa with a 1,300km railway

      <description><p>Rallies are planned at more than US 40 campuses as workers seeking better pay and conditions decry stalled talks</p><p>Starbucks baristas, students, elected officials and allies are planning rallies at <a href="https://starbucksworkersunited.controlshift.app/events?link_id=2&amp;can_id=debd8d2ad19f005d15f9bbdff314d42a&amp;source=email-nov-12-day-of-action-for-starbucks-baristas&amp;email_referrer=email_3490793&amp;email_subject=nov-12-day-of-action-for-starbucks-baristas&amp;&amp;">over 40 college campuses</a> across the US on Thursday to support the Starbucks Workers United <a href="https://www.boycottstarbucks.net/">boycott campaign</a> as the union nears five years of deadlock with the company over contract negotiations.</p><p>Starbucks Workers United is <a href="https://sbworkersunited.org/what-were-fighting-for-updates-on-contract-bargaining/">seeking</a> better pay and stronger staffing levels, including a $17 an hour minimum wage for baristas and a minimum staffing of three workers per store.       <description><p>Sales of built units fell to 3.75m in October, down by 8.8% from last year, with mortgage rates at nearly three-year high</p><p>US existing home sales hit a 16-year low in October as buyers were driven away by high <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/money/mortgage-rates">mortgage rates</a> and rising inflation, according to new data released on Wednesday.</p><p>Sales of already built units dropped to 3.75m in October, down by 8.8% from last year, the National Association of Realtors (NAR) <a href="https://www.nar.realtor/newsroom/existing-home-sales-decreased-5-5-percent-october-nar-report">reported</a>.       <title>Farewell to Elon Musk’s Cybertruck. Has any car ever been more repellent? | Arwa Mahdawi</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfree/2026/nov/11/farewell-cybertruck-elon-musk-car-repellent</link>
      <description><p>Safety campaigners have condemned it and owners have complained about it. Goodbye to a steel monstrosity seemingly designed by a five-year-old</p><p>Elon Musk is having a rough go of it, isn’t he? The world’s richest man spent almost half a billion dollars on the <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2026/nov/04/elon-musk-midterm-spending-analysis">midterms</a> in a failed attempt to defend Republican control of government. Now the tech mogul, who moved from California to Texas to escape Democrats and regulations, finds himself in a newly blue state. He also finds himself the subject of an unflattering <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/sep/08/musk-review-epic-study-worlds-richest-most-banal-man-elon-film">documentary</a> and, if the Democrats follow through on threats to investigate him, could potentially be in a spot of legal bother.</p><p>And to top it all off? Musk’s beloved Cybertruck, the steel monstrosity that looks as if it were designed by a five-year-old, is <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2026/nov/06/tesla-to-wind-down-cybertruck-production-as-elon-musk-focuses-on-robotics-and-ai">winding down production</a>. According to Musk, this isn’t because it’s an abject failure, but because he is channelling his energy into other things. “This is not a case of Cybertruck being unprofitable, as has been misreported by legacy media,” Musk <a href="https://x.com/elonmusk/status/2119691615774146614?a=pN3ISFVZZ-aU4_-TlJw&amp;s=20">tweeted</a> on Monday. “But rather that the opportunity cost of the complexity of Cybertruck is vastly outweighed by the value of incremental Cybercab production.” (The Cybercab is a two-passenger robotaxi.)</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfree/2026/nov/11/farewell-cybertruck-elon-musk-car-repellent">Continue reading...</a></description>

<![CDATA[Irish Times Feeds]]>https://www.irishtimes.comTue, 17 Nov 2026 00:56:41 +0000en1hourly1<![CDATA[Vast majority of Irish shoppers take dim view of Black Friday promises]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/17/vast-majority-of-irish-shoppers-take-dim-view-of-black-friday-promises/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/17/vast-majority-of-irish-shoppers-take-dim-view-of-black-friday-promises/Tue, 17 Nov 2026 00:01:00 +0000Irish consumers appear to be falling out of love with Black Friday, with fewer than one in four people trusting the discounts they are promised.

New research from the Competition and Consumer Protection Commission (CCPC) also suggests that the money people say they are likely to spend is falling dramatically, while almost one in five admit to drinking and shopping and making perhaps unwise decisions as a result.

The CCPC study found that only 23 per cent of Irish shoppers think retailers’ promises of big discounts can be believed, the lowest level recorded since the commission started tracking attitudes to Black Friday in 2022.

The national survey of 1,028 consumers also found that the average expected spend has fallen to €307 compared with €431 in 2024, with 47 per cent of consumers telling researchers that the cost of living has made them less likely to shop in Black Friday sales.

All told, 73 per cent of those polled said they did not trust that discounts are accurate, compared with 61 per cent when the survey began in 2022, while 80 per cent said they would carry out their own research to check on the accuracy of retailers’ promises before spending any money.

New laws against misleading discounts were introduced in 2022 and since then, the CCPC has successfully prosecuted several high-profile traders including Brown Thomas Arnotts, Boots, DID Electrical and Lifestyle Sports.

Men are likely to spend more than women, with the research suggesting they would spend €356 compared with the €269 likely to be spent by women. By contrast, 38 per cent of women said they were likely to purchase something during the sales compared with 31 per cent of men.

“Consumers no longer trust that Black Friday sales are an opportunity to save money and they are becoming much savvier about sales,” said the CCPC’s communications director Aoibhín de Búrca. “We’ve seen a noticeable decline in trust in discounts over the past five years; traders have some work to do to win back the trust of consumers.”

She added that the survey results show that many consumers are “shopping carefully, conscious of getting value for money and using their consumer rights to navigate high costs. They’re checking return policies, shopping within the EU, and showing a healthy degree of scepticism around flashy discount claims.”

The survey shows people are increasingly shopping exclusively online, while the number who have shopped online while under the influence of drugs or alcohol is close to 20 per cent. It also found that half admitted they regretted an impulse buy made during the sales.

More than half of shoppers report they will shop exclusively online, an increase of 13 per cent since 2024. A further 92 per cent of those planning to shop online in the sales intend to buy from traders based in Ireland.

“The good news for those who shop online and later regret their purchase is that as long as you’re buying from within the EU, you have 14 days to change your mind – and you’re entitled to a full refund if you do,” de Búrca said.

“Buying from Ireland or elsewhere in the EU means your consumer rights are stronger, plus you’ll avoid the new EU customs charge and union handling fee. Always check where your bargains are being shipped from; if it’s not clear, that’s a red flag.”

]]>Lisa Maree Williams<![CDATA[Bid to cross-examine McKillen jnr is attempt to exert pressure on businessman, court told]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/crime-law/courts/2026/11/16/bid-to-cross-examine-mckillen-jnr-is-attempt-to-exert-pressure-on-businessman-court-told/https://www.irishtimes.com/crime-law/courts/2026/11/16/bid-to-cross-examine-mckillen-jnr-is-attempt-to-exert-pressure-on-businessman-court-told/Mon, 16 Nov 2026 18:58:44 +0000Lenders owed a combined €11 million by Paddy McKillen jnr want to cross-examine the businessman to exert “maximum pressure” on him and his family and “generate a settlement”, his lawyers have told the High Court.

McKillen jnr is seeking a personal insolvency arrangement and has told the court he has debts of €27.7 million and is insolvent. In September the court granted him a protective certificate, which shields him from his creditors until at least December.

Lenders Herbert Street Finance and Cabriz Finance – who are owed €2.3 million and €8.7 million, respectively, by McKillen jnr – have both issued applications to set aside the protective certificate.

The applications arise from concerns raised by the lenders about an alleged material non-disclosure in information provided by McKillen jnr in his application for a protective certificate. McKillen jnr has rejected this allegation.

In a motion before Judge Nessa Cahill on Monday, lawyers for the two lenders sought various reliefs aimed at providing for the examination under oath of McKillen jnr on his financial affairs. Lawyers for McKillen jnr opposed the motion.

Bernard Dunleavy, for Herbert Street, told the judge his side was “not satisfied” with the financial information provided by McKillen jnr to the court.

Dunleavy, appearing with Niall Ó hUiginn, said the “elephant in the room” was what question McKillen jnr is concerned might be asked of him, and what answer he is worried might undermine his personal insolvency process.

Dunleavy submitted there were obligations on McKillen jnr to be of utmost good faith in his application for a protective certificate, as well as other statutory obligations to make “full and honest” disclosures relating to his financial affairs.

Dunleavy contended that McKillen jnr, in a submission, “almost put up to the court” that such declarations are a “box-ticking exercise”.

Counsel submitted that McKillen jnr, in this submission and in others, “turns his face away from the obligation he has to the court, on an ex parte application, of candour and utmost good faith”.

A separate entitlement to examine McKillen jnr on his affairs arises from a €2.3 million judgment entered in favour of Herbert Street against the businessman, Dunleavy submitted.

Martin Hayden, counsel for McKillen jnr, said the real purpose behind the application was to put “maximum pressure on Mr McKillen jnr and his family, to try and generate a settlement”.

Hayden, appearing with barrister Keith Farry, said the financial statement provided to the court during McKillen jnr’s application for a protective certificate was not defective.

Hayden said his client had addressed issues raised as concerns by the creditors.

To set aside a protective certificate, the creditors must show that they stand to suffer “irreparable harm”, Hayden submitted. The lenders have not done this, he contended.

He said the fact the lenders wanted a “deeper inquiry” did not warrant the application to cross-examine, or meet the threshold to set aside the certificate, he submitted.

Among the concerns raised by the creditors relates to debts owed by McKillen jnr to Jonc Ltd, an entity that is registered to an office where a McKillen jnr-linked company is also based, the court heard. McKillen jnr has denied any knowledge of the affairs of Jonc.

McKillen jnr was the co-founder of the hospitality group Press-Up.

The judge reserved her decision on the motion.

]]>w-ings<![CDATA[Tinder challenges €11m Data Protection Commission fine in High Court]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/16/tinder-challenges-11m-dpc-fine-in-high-court/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/16/tinder-challenges-11m-dpc-fine-in-high-court/Mon, 16 Nov 2026 17:58:03 +0000The provider of the online dating platform Tinder has brought a High Court challenge to an €11 million fine imposed by the Data Protection Commission (DPC) for failure to comply with its obligations in responding to requests for access to personal data by users of the service.

MTCH Technology Services Ltd is the provider of Tinder in the European Union, the European Economic Area, the United Kingdom and Switzerland.

MTCH says the primary purpose of Tinder is to “help people make meaningful connections and encourage users who meet online to meet offline or in real life”.

On October 13th last, the DPC found MTCH had failed to comply with its GDPR (General Data Protection Regulation) obligations in relation to requests for access by users of Tinder to personal data.

The DPC imposed an administrative fine of €11 million, issued a reprimand to MTCH and made an order requiring it to bring its processing into compliance.

On Monday, proceedings by MTCH challenging the fine were admitted to the High Court’s fast track Commercial Court on consent between the parties by Judge Eileen Roberts.

In an affidavit seeking entry of the proceedings to the list, Caroline Caffrey, MTCH senior manager, global escalations, said the grounds for its appeal were that the DPC made material errors of fact and law in its decision to impose an administrative fine.

MTCH contends these were manifest errors of assessment, including that the DPC had failed to establish that MTCH was negligent in committing the infringement of GDPR.

It also erred in law and acted outside its powers by applying European Data Protection Board guidelines on the application of administrative fines, among other reasons.

MTCH says the court should annul the decision to impose the fine and, should it consider appropriate, replace its own decision for that of the DPC.

]]>Jonathan Brady<![CDATA[Public service pay deal: What it means for someone on €30,000 or €60,000]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/politics/2026/11/14/public-service-pay-deal-what-it-means-for-a-special-needs-assistant-and-other-low-earners/https://www.irishtimes.com/politics/2026/11/14/public-service-pay-deal-what-it-means-for-a-special-needs-assistant-and-other-low-earners/Sat, 14 Nov 2026 06:00:00 +0000Thousands of special needs assistants (SNAs), clerical officers and other lower paid public sector workers are set to receive pay increases significantly beyond the 10.75 per cent headline figure in this week’s agreement between the Government and unions.

For anyone earning over €60,000 a year, that 10.75 per cent over two years and nine months will amount to 11.27 per cent when compounded.

For the very lowest paid public employees the uplift will exceed 18 per cent by March 2029. However, this example, provided by Government, of a newly recruited cleaner, is quite exceptional as the person would be one of the lowest earners in the entire public service.

An SNA with five years’ service will see their like-for-like income increase by 15.6 per cent over the term of the deal, while a newly recruited teacher, for example, will see a 12.75 per cent increase.

This assumes that they get the 1 per cent allocated for local bargaining, a mechanism for addressing sectoral or role-specific issues. This is not necessarily straight forward. All of the money may be allocated to a particular group of workers so they get significantly more than 1 per cent while others in the same sector get nothing. However, an even spread is assumed in the calculations given here.

Most employees in the public and Civil Service also benefit from annual increments during the early parts of their time in a particular role, an automatic annual increase linked to their growing experience.

In the case of SNAs, for instance, their pay would increase annually from €31,600 in year one to €47,300 in year 14 without any actual pay increases being received.

In the case of a principal officer on a higher scale, starting pay of €116,400 increases to €134,900 over five years. The number of increments depends on the role and these routinely provide substantial increases over time.

Such increments have been ignored for the purpose of these calculations, as have other elements of income, like allowances and overtime rates, many of which will be adjusted as a result of the new deal. In addition, figures have been rounded slightly for simplicity.

]]>Noreen M O Shea<![CDATA[Tribunal ruling sinks boat captains’ claims against marine staff agency]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/16/tribunal-ruling-sinks-boat-captains-claims-against-marine-staff-agency/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/16/tribunal-ruling-sinks-boat-captains-claims-against-marine-staff-agency/Mon, 16 Nov 2026 19:30:24 +0000A tribunal has found it has no jurisdiction to hear unfair dismissal claims pursued by two survey vessel captains against an employment agency which supplied staff to the national sea floor mapping project.

The Workplace Relations Commission (WRC) has rejected complaints by skippers Peter Cullen and Roy Jackson under the Unfair Dismissals Act 1977 against Dún Laoghaire Powerboat School Ltd, ruling both men were in fact employees of the Geological Survey of Ireland (GSI).

GSI, the State agency in charge of Infomar – a 20-year project that started in 2006 to map the sea floor around Ireland – had not been a party to the proceedings at the WRC.

At a hearing last December, adjudication officer Patricia Owens noted a preliminary objection from Dún Laoghaire Powerboat School to the effect that the men were not employees and therefore lacked standing to pursue the complaints against the firm.

The firm, a registered employment agency based at the south Dublin port, maintained the skippers were sole traders being paid by invoice for skippering Infomar survey vessels, and that it had contracts in place giving effect to this arrangement.

Jim Keegan, the powerboat school’s spokesman at the hearing, said it had contractual agreements in place with Cullen and Jackson as “sole traders or as a company” and that they had been paid in line with these contracts on foot of invoices.

“At no point have we paid PAYE or PRSI in terms of Mr Jackson or Mr Cullen,” Keegan said, adding that Cullen included VAT on his invoices.

Keegan told the tribunal that on foot of GSI tenders, the powerboat school won a series of one-year contracts starting in 2023 “to supply staff – skippers, surveyors, data processors” for the marine survey programme.

“They may have had someone from the GSI contact them with the possibility of employment – sorry, I shouldn’t say that word – the possibility of a contract,” Keegan said.

“The only contact we would have had is by email; we would have had people recommended to us and issued a contract if we’re satisfied they’re suitable for a position,” he said.

Keegan said the company was aware Cullen was a previous contractor with the GSI.

Leanne Fox, who represented both of the skippers, said the contracts were “bogus”.

Cullen, she said, had worked “directly for GSI” on the Infomar mapping operations “doing exactly the same job”.

“They forced him to go out to the powerboat school; he was then forced to sign the contract that was presented to them,” she said.

In her decisions on the men’s cases, published today, Owens found both Cullen and Jackson were “integral” to the Infomar project as vessel skippers.

Neither were “free to substitute” another worker instead of doing the work themselves, a key determining factor in the legal test for determining employment status.

It was clear, she added, that the time and place of the work were determined by the Geological Survey of Ireland.

The State agency, and not the powerboat school, provided the survey vessels used for the Infomar work, she added.

Owens found that Cullen and Jackson were agency workers – with the Dún Laoghaire Powerboat School being the employment agency, and GSI being the hirer or employer.

“In circumstances where the respondent is not the employer for the purposes of the Unfair Dismissals Act, on the basis of the preliminary matter, I find that this complaint is not well founded,” she concluded in both cases.

]]>Nick Bradshaw<![CDATA[Nvidia board not considering reappointing Jensen Huang despite Trump’s remarks]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/technology/big-tech/2026/11/16/jensen-huang-discusses-comeback-as-nvidia-ceo-with-allies/https://www.irishtimes.com/technology/big-tech/2026/11/16/jensen-huang-discusses-comeback-as-nvidia-ceo-with-allies/Mon, 16 Nov 2026 07:15:10 +0000Nvidia’s board is not considering reinstating Jensen Huang as the company’s chief executive, according to people familiar with the matter, despite US president Donald Trump saying he was open to such a move after the tech boss was ousted over an infidelity scandal.

The news marks the latest twist in the dramatic saga that has unfolded since it emerged that Huang had been engaged in an extramarital affair with a woman, Alice Huang, whom US intelligence officials believe was recruited to spy for China’s intelligence agency.

Huang resigned last week as the $4 trillion (€3.6 trillion) company’s board engaged in an independent inquiry into the spectacular leadership crisis. But a campaign among some leading tech figures to restore Huang had gathered steam, while the US president said on Monday he “wouldn’t mind” if he were reinstated.

The Financial Times reported on Sunday that Huang had discussed with confidants the possibility of returning to Nvidia.

The chipmaker’s board has said it will consider internal and external candidates for chief executive.

It was reported last week that the board had approached Arm chief executive Rene Haas in its search for a successor to Huang.
