The policy direction is clear. The National Planning Framework requires at least half of new housing in Dublin, Cork, Limerick, Galway and Waterford to be accommodated within their existing built-up areas. Government housing policy envisages more than 300,000 additional homes by 2030. Yet the places where we most want development to occur are frequently the most difficult and costly places in which to build.

Former industrial land, docklands, railway lands, redundant institutional sites and ageing inner-city districts often require land assembly, demolition, remediation, new streets, water and electricity infrastructure, schools, parks and public transport before substantial housing can be delivered.

Ireland therefore faces a fundamental contradiction. Planning policy is attempting to pull development inward while economics and infrastructure constraints continue to push it outwards.

This is why Copenhagen matters. Copenhagen’s remarkable transformation was not achieved primarily through enormous public subsidy. Its real innovation was institutional. Beginning in the 1990s, the Danish state and Copenhagen municipality brought substantial public landholdings into commercially managed development corporations, ultimately consolidated into CPH City & Port Development. These organisations combined public ownership with commercial discipline.

Public land was not simply sold to generate once-off receipts. It was treated as a strategic capital asset.

Planning increased its development potential. Infrastructure, particularly the Metro, increased its accessibility. That increased its value. The corporation could then borrow against that value, develop or lease land, enter joint ventures with private developers and pension funds, and recycle the proceeds into further infrastructure.

The sequence was straightforward. Public land was identified, comprehensive planning was undertaken, followed by infrastructure investment. This increased land value, which enabled development, value capture and reinvestment. It became what the Brookings Institution described as a virtuous cycle.

Perhaps the most important lesson is that Copenhagen put infrastructure in advance of development rather than waiting for development to justify infrastructure afterwards. The Metro fundamentally altered the value and attractiveness of Ørestad and later development areas.

More than 700 homes planned for Digital Hub lands in Dublin 8

Just as importantly, Copenhagen did not sell valuable public land prematurely. During the financial crisis it resisted pressure to dispose of assets cheaply. It used leases, rental income and joint ventures as well as outright sales, allowing the public sector to retain a share of the long-term value created by its own investment.

Ireland should not attempt to copy Copenhagen literally. But we should urgently apply its underlying principles. The striking fact is that Ireland already possesses most of the necessary instruments. We have the Land Development Agency (LDA), extensive publicly owned land, big housing programmes, regeneration funding, the €1 billion Housing Infrastructure Investment Fund, Croí Cónaithe, cost-rental supports, the Living City Initiative, vacancy and refurbishment schemes, the Residential Zoned Land Tax and planned investment in rail, Luas, MetroLink, water and energy infrastructure.

Our primary problem is no longer the absence of policy instruments. It is fragmentation. Land may be owned by one State body, planning controlled by another, transport delivered by another, water infrastructure provided by another and electricity capacity determined elsewhere. Housing funding and regeneration and transport investment are too often administered as separate programmes rather than assembled around the development of entire places. That must change.

Each of Ireland’s five cities should identify a small number – perhaps three to five – of strategic regeneration and transport-oriented development areas capable of accommodating housing and employment at genuinely significant scale.

For each city, the local authority and LDA should establish a long-term development partnership into which appropriate State lands can be transferred, leased or pooled. These partnerships should have multidisciplinary teams combining planning, property, infrastructure, finance and commercial development expertise.

Their purpose should not be to add another administrative layer. It should be to bring together functions that are at present divided. The first priority must be land assembly. Fragmented ownership should not be allowed to dictate the shape of our cities.

Bad news for Government: inflation triggers slowdown in construction

The second must be infrastructure certainty. Water, wastewater, electricity and public transport must be programmed before development rather than repeatedly emerging as reasons why development cannot proceed.

The third must be planning certainty. Detailed area plans should settle streets, densities, building heights, schools, parks, transport and infrastructure in advance. Development complying with those plans should then move through a substantially simpler consent process. Urban Development Zones under the Planning and Development Act 2024 could eventually become particularly valuable in this regard, but their potential must be translated rapidly into an operational system.

Most importantly, Ireland must rethink how it values public land. The maximum immediate sale price should not automatically be regarded as the best return to the taxpayer. Retaining land through long leases or joint ventures can generate housing, recurring income, infrastructure funding and decades of appreciation.

The same principle should apply to transport investment. MetroLink, DART+, Luas expansion and main rail corridors should be considered not merely transport projects but city-building projects. Where billions of euro of public investment create substantial increases in surrounding development capacity and land value, part of that value should systematically be captured for further infrastructure and affordable housing.

Time is becoming critical. Between now and 2030 Ireland must move from hundreds of disconnected schemes towards a limited number of big city-building programmes. During the 2030s, those programmes should mature into revolving investment systems in which the value created by one generation of development helps finance the next.

Deloitte’s housing hand grenade

Compact growth will not be achieved simply by putting higher-density targets into planning documents. Nor will our housing crisis be solved by repeatedly extending the edges of our cities. Successful compact cities require infrastructure, parks, schools, attractive public spaces, sustainable transport and places where people genuinely want to live. Copenhagen’s greatest lesson is therefore not architectural. It is institutional.

Ireland already has the land, the capital, the planning policies and most of the financial instruments required. What we still lack is a mechanism capable of combining them. Public land should cease to be viewed principally as property awaiting disposal. It should be regarded as strategic capital with which to build the next generation of Irish cities.

If we fail to make that change now, the consequences will be visible for decades in continuing housing shortages, worsening congestion, urban sprawl and missed regeneration opportunities. If we make it, Ireland has an opportunity to turn public investment into a permanent cycle of better infrastructure, more housing and stronger cities.

Designed to flatter their audience (humans), making us feel special, insightful and evolved, it is far preferable to that other scenario they sometimes set out: the end of the world.

So, it has been fascinating to witness this much-feted humanness on full display over the past 10 days. By that I mean Jensen Huang, cofounder and until a few days ago chief executive of Nvidia, the US semiconductor group underpinning the AI boom, who has been unfaithful to his wife of more than four decades, and the mother of his two children, with a woman who is allegedly a Chinese spy.

This was followed by new reports that Huang had an extramarital affair with a colleague, potentially breaching the company code of conduct. He resigned shortly afterwards.

Accountability – from voters, the board or shareholders – has a moderating effect on the powerful, says Joris Lammers, professor of political psychology at the University of Cologne, who has studied the relationship between power and infidelity.

Like alcohol, “power has a disinhibiting effect”, he told me, making those in charge “less focused on threats ... more inclined to do what they want [and] more inclined to infidelity”. More so than even the opportunities given by business travel.

Employers and educators have spotted a gap in the market for humans to gain an edge over AI by trying to encourage workers and students to hone their analytical skills or become better people. ]]>Imen Ben Youssef<![CDATA[Tea clubs and americanos better for productivity than Zoom and WFH]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/economy/2026/11/16/tea-breaks-and-productivity/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/economy/2026/11/16/tea-breaks-and-productivity/Mon, 16 Nov 2026 05:00:00 +0000Working from home at least part of the week has been a lasting effect of Covid for many office workers. It’s brought down the cost of commuting and made living a long distance from work more feasible. It’s provided flexibility for families around childcare. Overall, a third of the workforce now works from home either some or most of the time.

It’s not clear whether or not overall working time has been affected by this shift in work patterns. Data from employers suggest no change, while Labour Force Survey figures suggest men work on average an hour less a week than before the pandemic. However, because the respondents to that survey answer by phone, on behalf of all workers in their household, maybe some get that wrong.

Or possibly people include commuting time in perceived working hours, and that has clearly fallen.

While hybrid work is clearly popular – and more time in the office often resisted – the long-term impact on productivity is hard to establish. The common pattern, for example across much of the public service, of two days in the office and three days at home means that a minority of working time is spent being physically present with colleagues.

Engaging with people you already know well over Teams or Zoom video calls online is not necessarily a big challenge. Bringing new staff on board, and effective mentoring and managing of people who are largely working remotely, is much more difficult.

Hybrid working in Ireland expected to become less flexible over next two years, research suggests

“Sitting by Sally” was a traditional way for new workers to learn the ropes but it’s hard to pick up tips when Sally is working from her kitchen 30km away. It’s much easier to ask an experienced colleague what may be a trivial question if you run into them at the photocopier or pop over to their desk. New staff may be less likely to ask something they don’t know if it means sending an email or making a Zoom call. Where people are in or out on different core days, there may be some colleagues you never get to know at all.

So, given hybrid working, the informal bonds that help build a shared culture and knowledge in the workplace are now looser. One of the real casualties may be the cross-fertilisation of ideas and opportunities for collaboration.

The tea club was a key institution in the Department of Finance I joined in the 1970s. Those few rooms in Government Buildings that had a spare socket for a kettle were hosts to everyone in the section, from the typist to the assistant secretary general. While sport and political gossip provided much of the chat, in that 20 minutes a day there were also frequent discussions about economics that were like mini-seminars.

I learned a lot from colleagues who had studied abroad. Senior staff were generous with a rookie economist like myself when I floated maybe naive ideas.

How should a new recruit navigate a hybrid working system?

There was, initially, a different culture when I moved to the ESRI in the early 1980s. Like monks in their cells, researchers worked away in their rooms, and tea was delivered on a trolley lest you be distracted by chatting to colleagues.

I brought in a coffee percolator and would open my door at 11. The aroma attracted some exciting researchers who shared their ideas and insights over americanos.

Before long, the ESRI moved towards communal tea breaks, and over that period I can trace a growth in the number of research papers, and in collaborative authorship, as sharing ideas and pooling skills became the norm. The result was a big increase in productivity.

It’s not only in research or academia that working together produces more than working separately. Most workplaces require team working, sharing of experience and knowledge, and a positive culture of collaboration. They need people to spark off each other for new ideas, and that happens much more often in person than online.

From the employer side, hybrid working has allowed many to reduce their rent costs and office footprint. This often also involves moving to hot desking, where staff may have to find a different place to sit on each day they are in the office. It’s harder to build friendships and working relationships if you don’t know where Ciara will be sitting on a given day. Flexitime, where staff may only overlap for a few hours a week, also makes casual encounters with colleagues more difficult.

Hybrid working isn’t the problem, it is how to manage it

AI doesn’t do emotions and empathy, so coffee time becomes all the more important in helping build teams that enjoy working together. Six years after Covid, more time in the physical workplace might increase productivity.

]]><![CDATA[The Cybertruck flopped, but investors are still buying Musk’s moonshots]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/11/16/the-cybertruck-flopped-but-investors-are-still-buying-musks-moonshots/https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/11/16/the-cybertruck-flopped-but-investors-are-still-buying-musks-moonshots/Mon, 16 Nov 2026 05:00:00 +0000Elon Musk is fond of making grandiose predictions. Delivering them? Well, that’s another matter.

The Cybertruck, Tesla’s futuristic pick-up truck – was once touted as everything from a workhorse to a vehicle capable of travelling on Mars – is facing the end of the road. Musk says production will be wound down around the middle of 2027, barely three-and-a-half years after the first deliveries.

In 2023, Musk said an annual sales figure of 250,000 was a “reasonable guess”, adding it “might be 500,000”. However, the Cybertruck flopped. US sales almost halved in 2025, to 20,237, and fell below 12,000 in the first nine months of 2026.

To some extent, grand promises come with the territory for entrepreneurs – nothing ventured, nothing gained, and all that. However, the problem for Musk is how often they fail to materialise.

A New York Times investigation earlier this year examined 602 public goals and commitments Musk made over the previous 15 years. Just 19 per cent were achieved on schedule. Another 35 per cent were delivered late, sometimes by years, or never materialised.

For a further 33 per cent, there was no public update or insufficient information to establish whether they had been achieved. The remaining 13 per cent had deadlines still in the future.

His record also worsened over time: nearly three-quarters of his 2015 goals were met on schedule, compared with fewer than half by 2020.

Of course, Musk has also delivered some remarkable successes, but it’s hard to disagree with the FT’s Lex column, which described the Cybertruck as a masterclass in “failing upwards”.

Tesla Ireland’s chief on selling more cars, self-driving taxis and robots in our homes

Shares have slipped in 2026, but Tesla is still valued at $1.5 trillion – a hefty 12 times annual sales, while its price-to-earnings ratio is well into the hundreds.

Why? Max Gokhman of Franklin Templeton, which owns Tesla shares, says Musk has shown that “after long periods of missing deadlines, a moonshot may materialise”.

Perhaps that’s what Tesla – and SpaceX, Musk’s other extravagantly expensive stock – are: moonshot stocks, where investors overlook repeated disappointments in the hope of an eventual breakthrough.

]]>Justin Sullivan<![CDATA[Irish domestic demand growth to accelerate to 4% next year, Ibec says]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/16/irish-domestic-demand-growth-to-accelerate-to-4-next-year-ibec-says/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/16/irish-domestic-demand-growth-to-accelerate-to-4-next-year-ibec-says/Mon, 16 Nov 2026 00:01:00 +0000Irish domestic demand, a measure of the economy that strips out the impact of multinationals, is on track to grow by 4 per cent next year, despite mounting global pressures from volatile energy prices and rising interest rates, according to Ibec.

]]><![CDATA[No, people have not fallen out of love with work]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/work/2026/11/15/no-people-have-not-fallen-out-of-love-with-work/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/work/2026/11/15/no-people-have-not-fallen-out-of-love-with-work/Sun, 15 Nov 2026 10:00:00 +0000Have people lost the will to work? This theory – until now quite wishy-washy – appeared to gain some quantitative heft in the UK last week thanks to the latest edition of the long-running British Social Attitudes Survey.

The results revealed the lowest job satisfaction in the survey’s history and a broad-based decline since 2015 in the proportion of employees who said they were willing to work harder than was required to help their employer succeed. A rising share of Britons said they would prefer to work fewer than full-time hours, driven by men (both fathers and non-fathers).

This has revived a debate that took place in the aftermath of the pandemic, when young workers posted on TikTok about “quiet quitting” their jobs, while overworked youth in China spoke of “tang ping” (or “lying flat”). Some theorised that people no longer wanted to toil in a “bullshit job” that didn’t contribute to society, in the words of social anthropologist David Graeber.

But it is worth examining the rest of the data. The share of people who say they would prefer not to work at all remains a very low and stable 4 per cent. So why might they want to work less? It is not because they think their jobs are “bullshit”.

In fact, the proportion who say their job is useful to society has risen steadily from 54 per cent in 1989 to 73 per cent in 2025 – the highest in the survey’s history.

Nor is it because people have lost all ambition and drive. The workforce’s largest “unmet wants” in 2025 – the gap between the proportion of people rating a certain work attribute as important and those reporting that they actually have it – were for a high income and advancement opportunities. Both of these gaps have widened since 2015. This does not smack of a country that just wants to slack off.

But it does point to a more straightforward reason for people’s decreased willingness to go above and beyond for their employers: not enough money and progression.

Real weekly earnings in the UK have risen overall since 2015, but they’re still barely above where they were in 2008 after a dreadful decade and a half for living standards.

On top of that, the proportion of respondents who said their job had good opportunities for advancement fell from 35 to 26 per cent.

This fits with stories I hear from UK workers and employers about wage compression on the lower rungs due to the rising minimum wage, and from white-collar managers who complain they have to rate each team member’s performance on a forced-distribution curve, even if no one has performed badly.

How ‘workfluencers’ became the new buttoned-up breed of content creator

I suspect there is something else at play, too. We know from a different long-running data set – the Skills and Employment Survey – that Britons have experienced a remarkable loss of autonomy at work over recent years.

In 1992, 62 per cent of surveyed workers said they had a great deal of discretion over which tasks to do and how to do them. By 2024, only 34 per cent said the same.

This decline was initially most evident among people in lower-paid jobs, but between 2017 and 2024, “task discretion” fell among professionals and more highly skilled workers too. This does not appear to be UK-specific: a large continuing survey of workers across Europe has found “a concerning decrease in workers’ ability to influence collective work processes and apply their own ideas”.

My employer cuts maternity top-up payments by half after three months. Is the norm not six months of full pay?

I have begun to think of this as the “routinisation” of professional work. Why has it happened? When I last wrote about the phenomenon, I heard from many readers with whom it resonated. Most of them attributed the trend to increased regulatory demands and technology, which had made it easier for employers to codify, structure and monitor people’s work.

Some pointed out the benefits: allowing less leeway for personal discretion can make for more consistency and fewer mistakes – particularly important in safety-critical sectors such as medicine.

But I also heard from those who said their jobs had become more frustrating and less fun, from academics tied up in bureaucracy to tech workers who said so-called “agile” working practices had morphed into the opposite.

Employers have no doubt been quick to measure the gains of this routinisation process. Now we are beginning to see the costs. It’s not hard to understand why, if you have little control over how you work, you might feel less willing or able to go above and beyond.

Britons haven’t fallen out of love with work itself. They just don’t love to work like this. – The Financial Times Limited 2026

]]>Isbjorn<![CDATA[Markets still pricing in two more ECB rate hikes]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/15/markets-still-pricing-in-two-more-ecb-rate-hikes/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/15/markets-still-pricing-in-two-more-ecb-rate-hikes/Sun, 15 Nov 2026 06:00:00 +0000Markets are pricing in at least two more European Central Bank interest rate hikes even with the sharp drop-off in oil prices and the improving inflationary outlook.

ECB officials are expected to increase the deposit rate by a quarter-point to 2.75 per cent at their final monetary-policy meeting of 2026. This will push interest rates to the top of a range that is deemed to be neutral (neither stoking nor restricting economic activity).

Franfurt has raised borrowing costs twice since the conflict in the Middle East pushed energy prices sharply higher.

With inflation now running at twice the ECB’s 2 per cent target level, Klaas Knot, one of two contenders to become the next ECB chief, said this week the bank’s interest rate policy was likely to remain hostage to developments in the Middle East and their impact on energy prices.

He said that if energy prices remained roughly where they were, he saw little need for higher interest rates. “There may be a bit of extra tightening needed, but I don’t think an awful lot of it,” Knot said, adding that any interest rate changes needed to be “very measured”.

Another factor paving the way for another rate hike is euro zone growth, which has been more resilient in the face of inflation that many had predicted, helped in part by multinational exports from Ireland.

Gross domestic product (GDP) across the 21-member currency bloc rose 0.4 per cent in the third quarter, Eurostat said on Friday, matching an initial estimate from October.

This gives the central bank more leeway to counteract inflation with growth-anchoring interest rates.

The global economy is by no means out of the woods on inflation given the ongoing impasse in the Middle East.

Bond market turmoil is also expected to weigh on the growth as countries struggle to service their debts.

The ECB sees growth risks as tilted to the downside and those for inflation as skewed to the upside.

]]>Ben Kilb<![CDATA[Why Anthropic’s IPO is nothing like Google’s]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/11/15/why-anthropics-ipo-is-nothing-like-googles/https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/11/15/why-anthropics-ipo-is-nothing-like-googles/Sun, 15 Nov 2026 06:00:00 +0000Anthropic still plans to go public next week, despite recent volatility in AI stocks and a sharp reassessment of its prospective valuation. After investors contemplated as much as $2 trillion (€1.8 trillion) only weeks ago, figures ranging from $1.1 trillion to $1.5 trillion have since been floated.

The valuation wobble has irked at least one investor.

“If [public market investors] are not seeing the narrative at this point, they are failing a basic IQ test,” one early Anthropic backer told the Financial Times. “The next Google is dancing naked in front of you. If you can’t see the value of it, you don’t deserve to make money.”

Anthropic may be dancing naked in front of investors, to stick with this unfortunate metaphor, but it may also be asking them to pay some $1.5 trillion for the privilege of watching.

As for Google, it was valued at $23 billion when it floated in 2004 – less than Yahoo, then valued at $39 billion. In contrast, Anthropic’s trillion-dollar status will immediately place it among the S&P 500’s most valuable companies.

Put another way, $1.5 trillion would buy 65 Googles at their 2004 valuation. Even $1 trillion would buy 43. The two opportunities are hardly comparable.

Anthropic may well be worth $1.5 trillion or more. It may outperform in coming years. However, there is only so much excitement in the prospect of buying the “next Google” when it is already valued as though it has achieved Google’s success.

]]>Gabby Jones

The historic St Mary’s Basilica in Kraków has hosted a holy mass for Michał Oksiński, the man who carried out the recent attack in the city and later died of injuries sustained in a shootout with police.

The six people who died in the attack and more than a dozen who were injured were shot by Oskiński on the square where the church stands, some of them just a few metres from its doors.

St Mary’s Basilica says that the mass is “an expression of the Christian faith in God’s mercy” and “in no way indicates justification for the crime”.

On the afternoon of 7 November, Oksiński launched his attack on Kraków’s famous market square, which was packed with locals and tourists. He shot at random from his car while driving through the square and surrounding streets before police managed to bring his rampage to an end.

Later that same day, the dead bodies of Oksiński’s parents and sister were found in his home. They had each been shot in the head while sleeping. Two days after the attack, Oskiński himself died in hospital.

On Sunday, Łukasz Wantuch, a former city councillor, shared a photograph of an announcement that there would be “a holy mass for the late Michał Oksiński and the deceased members of his family” at the Roman Catholic St Mary’s Basilica on Monday morning.

The church, built in the 14th century, is one of the most famous in Poland and dominates the skyline in Kraków’s historic, UNESCO-listed city centre. It stands on one corner of the market square, just a few steps from where some of Oksiński’s victims were shot.

“I won’t hide the fact that I find this somewhat shocking,” wrote Wantuch. He noted that the announcement referred to the “blessed memory” (świętej pamięci) of Oksiński. However, that phrase is standard usage in Polish to refer to someone who has died (the equivalent ot the English “late”).

“But perhaps that is what faith is about: praying even for a murderer,” added Wantuch. Among the more than 1,000 comments under his Facebook post, many agreed with that sentiment.

“The whole of Christianity is based on forgiving the unforgivable,” wrote one. “I don’t think anyone needs God’s mercy more [than Oksiński],” said another.

However, some others were critical of the fact that the mass was being held in that particular church among the dozens in Kraków. “It is the height of impudence that they’ll celebrate mass for him in the very church he murdered in front of,” wrote one commenter.

 

Later on Sunday, St Mary’s Basilica issued a statement, signed by parish administrator Father Mariusz Słonina, saying that the holy mass “is a private initiative of one of the priests, not of St Mary’s Parish”.

However, Słonina added that “praying for the deceased is an expression of the Christian faith in God’s mercy” and “in no way indicates justification for the crime, a lessening of the perpetrator’s responsibility, or a trivialisation of the suffering of the victims”.

Local news service KR24 reported that uniformed police officers were posted outside the church for today’s mass while plainclothes officers were inside, with one of them right next to the altar.

Three priests were present, including Słonina, who presided over the mass. Only around a dozen faithful were in attendance, with KR24 suggesting that many did not even seem aware for whom mass was being held.

Separate private funeral ceremonies will take place for Oksiński, his parents and sister, who lived in the town of Ostrowiec Świętokrzyski, about 160 km from Krakow. On Sunday, their family issued a statement asking the media to “respect the privacy, dignity and mourning of our family and loved ones”.

Meanwhile, police and prosecutors continue to investigate the possible motive behind Oksiński’s attack, which they are treating as a terrorist offence. Last week, the justice minister said that there were “very strong traces of right-wing extremism” in the perpetrator’s online activity.

Two police officers, Jakub Kulik and Artur Morański, who were seriously injured in the shootout that debilitated Okisński, have been recovering in hospital after undergoing emergency surgery.

Poland has detained and charged three teenagers who are allegedly linked to “an international neo-Nazi network” and had been planning terrorist attacks, including with the use of homemade explosives.

The arrests were announced on Monday morning by Tomasz Siemoniak, the minister in charge of the security services, who revealed that the suspects are Polish citizens. Two are aged 17 and one is 16.

“The teenagers not only promoted Nazi and fascist ideology but had also already taken steps toward committing terrorist offences,” wrote Siemoniak.

Funkcjonariusze @ABW_GOV_PL zatrzymali 3 obywateli RP, 16-latka i dwóch 17-latków, związanych z międzynarodowym środowiskiem neonazistowskim.
▶️ Nastolatkowie nie tylko propagowali ideologię nazistowską i faszystowską, ale podejmowali już działania zmierzające do popełniania…

— Tomasz Siemoniak (@TomaszSiemoniak) November 16, 2026

The National Prosecutor’s Office revealed that the trio were “fascinated by the activities of an international neo-Nazi terrorist organisation…[that] has an ideology based on hatred against people of Jewish descent, immigrants, black people, the LGBT community, politicians and state security officials”.

Though prosecutors did not name the organisation, they said that members of it have been involved in planning terrorist attacks in the United States, Germany and the United Kingdom. In some countries, including the UK, Canada and Australia, it has been outlawed and designated a terrorist group.

Poland’s Internal Security Agency (ABW) had found that the three suspects’ online communication indicated “an interest in constructing explosive devices, modifying weapons and using such items to carry out terrorist activities”.

During a search of the home of one of the 17-year-olds (named only as “suspect 1”), officers found chemicals that are precursors for the production of explosives. That suspect has also been charged with possession of a so-called pipe bomb, which prosecutors say he wanted to “transfer to a neo-Nazi terrorist group”.

 

Suspect 1 was found to have discussed with the other 17-year-old, named as suspect 2, how to construct an explosive device and detonate it in a specific residential building where someone they knew lived.

Suspect 1 had also “incited extremist behaviour and hate-motivated violence” in his online activity, while the 16-year-old, named as suspect 3, had “promoted fascist content” (a crime in Poland) and encouraged someone to assault another person based on their race.

Each suspect has been charged with three crimes, relating variously to terrorist offences, possession or attempted production of explosives and weapons, promoting Nazism, fascism and racial hatred, and inciting others to commit violence based on racial differences.

Prosecutors note that Polish law generally allows people to face full criminal liability from the age of 17. The two 17-year-olds have therefore been placed in adult pretrial detention, while the 16-year-old is being held in a juvenile facility.

Śledztwo w sprawie neonazistów i planowanych aktów terroru kryminalnego

Szczegóły w komunikacie: ⬇️https://t.co/dQpdgiTYJD

— Prokuratura Regionalna w Gdańsku (@Prok_Regio_GDA) November 16, 2026

The arrests come in the context of recent concerns over radicalisation of young people in Poland. Earlier this month, a 24-year-old carried out a terrorist attack in the city of Kraków, killing six people by firing a rifle from his car. He had earlier killed his parents and sister in their home.

In the aftermath of the attack, justice minister Waldemar Żurek revealed that investigators had found “very strong traces of right-wing extremism” in the attacker’s online activity, though he emphasised that the motive was yet to be determined.

In the space of a few days last month, three knife attacks took place in Polish schools, resulting in one case in the death of a member of staff. Dozens of young people were arrested in the aftermath for making threats and/or possessing weapons.

In September, the security services detained three teenagers accused of being part of online groups promoting neo-Nazism and violence. One of them has been charged with planning terrorist attacks on targets including a mosque and a school.

Around a dozen public monuments in Poland, including one dedicated to the Warsaw Ghetto Uprising, have been defaced with graffiti glorifying the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA), a World War Two nationalist partisan group that was responsible for the massacre of Poles and Jews.

Ukraine’s embassy in Warsaw has condemned the vandalism and blamed it on Russia, which has previously been accused by the Polish authorities of orchestrating provocative graffiti on monuments.

W sobotę, 14 listopada, w Warszawie doszło do kolejnych dwóch dewastacji pomników. Napisy „Slava UPA” pojawiły się na Pomniku Bohaterów Getta przed Muzeum Historii Żydów Polskich POLIN oraz na Pomniku Żołnierzy 1 Armii Wojska Polskiego przy ulicy Andersa 13. To kolejna odsłona… pic.twitter.com/Y7NDsfpjxn

— Miejski Reporter (@MiejskiReporter) November 14, 2026

The latest spate of vandalism was first reported in early November in the western city of Poznań, where three World War two memorials were painted with graffiti saying “Glory to the UPA” (Slawa UPA).

While the UPA is remembered by many in Ukraine for fighting for independence from Moscow-imposed Soviet rule, in Poland it is primarily associated with leading the Volhynia massacres, in which around 100,000 Polish civilians, mostly women and children, were slaughtered as part of an ethnic cleansing operation.

Local police in Poznań told the Gazeta Wyborcza daily that they were searching for a young man dressed in black who is believed to be the culprit, but have so far not been able to identify him.

 

Similar graffiti was subsequently reported on seven monuments, including ones dedicated to Polish World War Two heroes and anti-communist protests that took place in 1970, in Gdańsk and Gdynia, neighbouring cities on Poland’s northern Baltic coast.

On Friday, local police in Gdańsk confirmed that they had detained a 17-year-old Ukrainian on suspicion of “painting offensive slogans propagating hatred”. They shared blurred-out images of the suspect as well as cans of spray paint.

He has been charged with promoting fascist ideology, incitement to violence and hatred based on nationality, and desecration of monuments. If convicted, he could face up to three years in prison.

Previously, on Tuesday this week, MOST, a Polish-based Belarusian independent media outlet, published findings that an anonymous person on messaging service Telegram, which is popular among Russians, Ukrainians and Belarusians, had been offering $500 plus travel expenses for a job in Poznań.

When an undercover MOST journalist responded to the advert, he was told that the job would involve spray painting “Glory to the UPA” on monuments. The recruiter confirmed that the job was illegal, “but if you cover your face and do everything quickly, they won’t find you”.

They also revealed that similar jobs were available in other Polish cities, including Warsaw, Wrocław and Lublin.

Subsequently, similar inscriptions appeared in Warsaw on the Monument to the Ghetto Heroes, which honours the Jews who rose up against their German-Nazi oppressors in 1943; a monument commemorating the Polish First Army, which fought in World War Two; and a monument to sappers who served in the war.

The vandalism was condemned by Poland’s Jewish Historical Institute (ŻIH), which called it a “disgraceful attack on the memory of the victims of the Holocaust and the heroes of Jewish resistance”.

Noting MOST’s findings and the vandalism of other monuments, ŻIH said that “this points to the possibility of an organised provocation intended to incite hatred and divide society”.

Warsaw police told PAP that they are investigating and seeking to identify the perpetrator. An unnamed police source also told Gazeta Wyborcza they see the incidents in all four cities as related to one another, pointing to the similar style of the inscriptions.

On Sunday afternoon, Warsaw’s mayor, Rafał Trzaskowski, condemned the vandalism and shared images of the municipal authorities cleaning the graffiti off the Ghetto Heroes Monument.

“Given the scale of similar incidents in other cities, we must consider the possibility that this is a planned provocation,” added the mayor. “Let us not let ourselves be divided – the authorities are working to identify both those who carried out these acts and those who ordered them.”

Nie ma zgody na wandalizm w Warszawie.

Minionej nocy służby miejskie wyczyściły pomniki oszpecone przez wandali – między innymi Pomnik Bohaterów Getta. Sprawców szuka policja.

Patrząc na skalę podobnych incydentów w innych miastach, musimy brać pod uwagę, że mamy do czynienia… pic.twitter.com/5xMgPhnHf8

— Rafał Trzaskowski (@trzaskowski_) November 15, 2026

A day earlier, on Saturday, the Ukrainian embassy had also condemned the acts of vandalism, calling them a “disgraceful provocation”.

“In our view, these unlawful acts are a manifestation of the hybrid war that Russia is attempting to wage by any means in European states, and in Poland in particular,” wrote the embassy. “The objective is clear: to incite hostility between Poles and Ukrainians, undermine mutual trust, and weaken support for Ukraine.”

Writing in both Polish and Ukrainian, the embassy appealed to Ukrainians “not to be tempted by offers of ‘easy money’ in exchange for painting graffiti, damaging property, or carrying out other illegal tasks” and to report any such offers to the Polish police.

“Let us respect the laws of the country in which we reside, as well as historical memory and each other’s dignity,” they added. “Polish-Ukrainian solidarity is our shared strength. Let us not allow the enemy to destroy it.”

Poland has been a primary target for Russia’s so-called hybrid actions in Europe, which have included acts of sabotage, espionage, disinformation and efforts to stir hostility towards Ukrainians.

Such operations are rarely carried out by Russian operatives themselves. Instead, Russia often recruits people already on the ground, often members of Poland’s large Ukrainian and Belarusian migrant communities, as well as Poles themselves in some cases.

In July this year, a Ukrainian teenager was indicted by Polish prosecutors on charges of painting dozens of pro-UPA slogans in public places, including on a monument to victims of the Volhynia massacres.

An 18-year-old Ukrainian will stand trial in Poland accused of working on behalf of Russia to stir tension between Poland and Ukraine by painting dozens of inscriptions in public places glorifying the Ukrainian Insurgent Army, which massacred Poles in WWII https://t.co/0w0gVYiGpp

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 16, 2026

There have long been tensions between Poland and Ukraine over the massacres, which Poland recognises as a genocide. Ukraine rejects that label, and also continues to honour the UPA for its role in fighting for independence.

The issue has recently flared up again this year after President Volodymyr Zelensky named a Ukrainian military unit after the “heroes of the UPA”. That sparked widespread anger in Poland and prompted Polish President Karol Nawrocki to strip Zelensky of his country’s highest honour.

President Karol Nawrocki has vetoed a government bill creating new powers to block harmful online content. Nawrocki, who is aligned with the right-wing opposition, argued that the measures were too far-reaching and could be abused to introduce “censorship”.

Government figures have strongly criticised the president’s decision, arguing that it will leave young people in particular more exposed to dangerous content. It also means that Poland still has not fully implemented the European Union’s Digital Services Act (DSA).

❌ Nie dla cenzury Internetu! pic.twitter.com/WusnK7LImD

— Kancelaria Prezydenta RP (@prezydentpl) November 13, 2026

Previously, in January this year, Nawrocki had vetoed an earlier bill intended to implement the DSA, describing the measures as “Owellian”.

That prompted the government to split the legislation in two. In September, Nawrocki agreed to sign one of those bills, which appointed the president of the Office of Electronic Communications (UKE) as Poland’s digital services coordinator, responsible for overseeing enforcement of the DSA.

A second bill was then needed to introduce the actual powers to block harmful online content. In October, it was approved in parliament by the ruling coalition, which ranges from left to centre right. The right-wing and far-right opposition either voted against it or abstained.

 

Among the new powers included in the legislation were authorisation for the heads of UKE and the National Broadcasting Council (KRRiT) to order the blocking of online content containing violence or threats based on race, nationality, ethnicity, religion or political affiliation.

It also allowed the immediate blocking, at the request of a prosecutor or the police, of content involving the acceptance of a contract to commit murder or inciting or assisting in suicide or self-harm.

“Perpetrators of serious crimes should not be allowed to use the internet to spread violence and threats,” said digital affairs minister Krzysztof Gawkowski. “The state must have effective tools to quickly respond to such threats. The safety of internet users must transcend political divisions.”

The government also argued that last month’s series of stabbings in schools and this month’s deadly terrorist attack in Kraków – which have raised concern about the online radicalisation of young people – have emphasised the importance of tough controls over digital content.

There are "strong traces of right-wing extremism" in the activity of the man who carried out the mass shooting in Kraków, says Poland's justice minister.

His search history included websites relating to Anders Breivik, the Norwegian far-right terrorist https://t.co/UhVbkWSaCq

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) November 10, 2026

However, on Friday, the final day by which the president had to make a decision on the bill, Nawrocki announced that he was vetoing it. He argued that “the government has clearly mixed up European obligations with its own political interests”.

The measures in the bill threaten to create a “censorship official” and “essentially give the government arbitrary control and the ability to decide what we can and cannot say, write or publish, said the president.

Decisions on whether content is permitted or not should be “the exclusive competence of the justice system and independent judges”, he argued. Nawrocki also said that the powers in the vetoed bill were “disproportionate”, allowing an entire domain to be blocked due to a single example of illegal content.

“The security of citizens cannot be a pretext for weakening their freedoms,” said Nawrocki. “We must not create a false choice: either the security or the freedom of its citizens. A responsible state must ensure and balance both.”

Dlaczego Prezydent RP Karol Nawrocki zawetował ustawę o DSA? ⬇️ pic.twitter.com/1BUJVFEftl

— Kancelaria Prezydenta RP (@prezydentpl) November 13, 2026

Deputy digital affairs minister Dariusz Standerski, however, said that the president was “not defending free speech” but instead “once again siding with global [digital] platforms and allowing them to decide what users see”.

“The vetoed provisions concerned illegal content, not opinions or views expressed online,” added the ministry, which also noted that all decisions on blocking content were subject to appeals and judicial review.

Prime Minister Donald Tusk, meanwhile, accused Nawrocki of “waging war on the government at the expense of Polish children and Polish security”, which would both be threatened by the absence of the vetoed measures.

Z prezydenckiego weta zadowoleni są hejterzy, rosyjskie farmy trolli, pedofile, ekstremalni nihiliści i lobbyści. Ofiarami tego weta są polskie dzieci, rodzice, bezpieczeństwo wszystkich obywateli. Tego nie da się w żaden sposób usprawiedliwić.

— Donald Tusk (@donaldtusk) November 14, 2026

Aleksandra Wójtowicz, an analyst on new technologies at the Polish Institute of International Affairs (PISM), told the Fakt newspaper that the measures do “not in any way relate to alleged censorship”. They are intended to force digital platforms to remove illegal content, she explained.

Wójtowicz added that the measures would actually have protected free speech by giving Polish users whose accounts were unjustly deleted by social media platforms the right to appeal against those decisions outside of the platform itself.

However, Nawrocki’s veto was praised by Przemysław Czarnek, deputy leader of the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS), Poland’s largest opposition party. Czarnek told TV Trwam that the proposed measures had been intended to “fight the opposition” rather than actual hate speech.

A new hub has opened at the University of Oxford to support research cooperation with Poland, offering grants for academic projects, visits, training and workshops.

The Oxford Poland Hub, which its organisers describe as Poland’s first initiative of its kind anywhere in the world, will also hold public events exploring Polish history, language and culture.

Huge thanks to:
🔹 @UniofOxford & @JesusOxford, esp. Prof Paulina Kewes & Dr Marek Naczyk
🔹 Ministry of Science and Higher Education & Minister @MarcinKulasek 🧵 pic.twitter.com/LghfpOhptC

— Polish Embassy UK 🇵🇱 (@PolishEmbassyUK) November 12, 2026

“The launch of the Oxford-Poland Hub is an exciting new chapter in Oxford’s longstanding relationship with Poland,” said the University of Oxford’s vice-chancellor, Irene Tracey. “[It] will create new opportunities for academic exchange, collaborative research and partnership between Oxford and Poland.”

The centre is initially funded for three years by Poland’s National Agency for Academic Exchange (NAWA), with support from the science and higher education ministry. It will operate within The Oxford Research Centre in the Humanities (TORCH).

“The Oxford Poland Hub…gives us a permanent institutional presence at one of the world’s leading academic centres,” said Wojciech Karczewski, NAWA’s director general.

“We see it as an investment in long-term partnerships that will enable researchers from Poland and Oxford to tackle increasingly ambitious research challenges together.”

 

The University of Oxford is the oldest university in the English-speaking world and one of the most prestigious. It ranked first globally in the latest Times Higher Education World University Rankings.

The new centre will offer grants of up to £5,000 (26,400 zloty) to support research projects or academic visits and up to £10,000 for academic workshops. Training scholarships are due to be introduced from the hub’s second year.

All researchers affiliated with the University of Oxford will be eligible to apply for funding if their work involves collaboration with researchers based in Poland. The hub will focus on humanities and social sciences as well as cooperation with Oxford’s libraries and museums.

The hub will also organise public lectures, exhibitions and events related to Polish history, language and culture for the academic community and Oxford’s residents, including its Polish community.

🇵🇱🇬🇧 Oxford-Poland Hub oficjalnie otwarty! Polska nauka zyskuje nowe możliwości współpracy z Uniwersytetem Oksfordzkim.

W uroczystym otwarciu wziął udział minister nauki i szkolnictwa wyższego Marcin Kulasek. Centrum powstało dzięki współpracy Ministerstwa Nauki i Szkolnictwa… pic.twitter.com/bZaCdM3Y53

— Ministerstwo Nauki i Szkolnictwa Wyższego (@MNiSW_GOV__PL) November 10, 2026

The hub was inaugurated on Monday at Jesus College, one of Oxford University’s colleges, with Poland’s science and higher education minister, Marcin Kulasek, and Rafał Wiśniewski, chargé d’affaires at the Polish Embassy in London, among those attending.

“Poland and the United Kingdom have for many years developed strong cooperation in science and higher education through joint research projects, academic mobility programmes and institutional partnerships,” Kulasek said. “The Oxford–Poland Hub opens a new chapter in this cooperation.”

The centre is directed by Paulina Kewes, a professor of English literature at Oxford who was born in Poland. Professor Norman Davies, the renowned historian of Poland and an honorary fellow at St Antony’s College, Oxford, attended the launch.

The inaugural lecture, given by Dariusz Wójcik, a professor at the National University of Singapore and honorary research associate at the University of Oxford, discussed Maria Czaplicka, the renowned Polish academic who in 1916 became Oxford’s first female lecturer of anthropology.

A Belgian court has overturned an order to seize funds from Poland’s air-traffic control agency, PANSA, as part of pharmaceutical giant Pfizer’s efforts to enforce a €1.3 billion claim for COVID-19 vaccines Poland ordered but later refused to receive and pay for.

The ruling, issued on Thursday, followed a legal challenge by PANSA to the freezing of its funds. It argued that it was not a party to the dispute between Pfizer and the Polish state.

❗️Dziś Francuskojęzyczny Sąd Pierwszej Instancji w Brukseli wydał korzystny dla strony polskiej wyrok w sprawie zajęcia opłat trasowych należnych @PANSA_PL , pobieranych za pośrednictwem EUROCONTROL.

Sąd uznał zajęcie za bezzasadne i uchylił postanowienie, na podstawie którego… pic.twitter.com/EHvHZnL6ab

— Ministerstwo Zdrowia (@MZ_GOV_PL) November 12, 2026

In July this year, PANSA announced that it had been cut off from the fees paid to it by the European Organisation for the Safety of Air Navigation (Eurocontrol), which manages air traffic in Europe. Around 80% of PANSA’s revenue comes from those fees.

Eurocontrol is based in Belgium, which is where Pfizer has been fighting its legal battle against Poland over the unpaid vaccines. The move to freeze PANSA’s funds was part of Pfizer’s efforts to claim money it had been awarded from Poland by a Belgian court in April this year.

Prime Minister Donald Tusk pledged government support to ensure PANSA had sufficient funds to maintain its operations and assured that air safety would not be compromised.

Poland’s air-traffic control agency has been cut off from most of its revenue as part of efforts by pharmaceutical giant Pfizer to enforce a Belgian court ruling requiring Poland to pay €1.3bn for Covid vaccines it ordered but then refused to receive https://t.co/Nd9IyLqmmf

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 11, 2026

On Thursday this week, PANSA announced that its legal challenge to the seizure of its assets by bailiffs had been successful, though it noted that the ruling can still be appealed.

Poland’s health ministry, which has been involved in overseeing the legal battle with Pfizer, said that the Belgian court had confirmed that PANSA’s funds belong to the agency itself, not to the State treasury.

“The agency is a separate legal entity; it possesses its own assets and manages its own finances independently. It is not liable for the obligations of the State treasury; therefore, its funds cannot be used to satisfy Pfizer’s claims against Poland,” wrote the ministry.

 

In comments to Polish Radio, PANSA chief Magdalena Jaworska-Maćkowiak said the agency had become a hostage in a case “that did not, in fact, concern us”.

By Leo Greenberg

Speaking to Fox News in late October, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky admitted a widely known but uncomfortable truth: Ukraine needs its refugees back.

“We need 9.5 million people – who lost their homes, who are abroad, everywhere – we need them to come back to Ukraine…to rebuild their country,” he said.

Zelensky:

We need 9.5 million people who lost their housing, who are abroad everywhere — we need them to come back to Ukraine, just to live and to build their country. pic.twitter.com/Xu2Ld4eGOu

— Clash Report (@clashreport) October 21, 2026

Unfortunately for Ukraine, all signs point in the opposite direction: Ukrainians abroad are deferring or abandoning thoughts of return.

A large proportion of those refugees – almost one million of them – live in Poland, where Ukrainians, including migrants who arrived before 2022, have provided an economic and demographic boon. But their continued stay has also posed social and political challenges, as a country with no history of mass immigration grapples with the new reality of a sizable non-citizen minority.

This has left the refugees themselves in a state of limbo: torn between a homeland that wants them back, and to which many would like to return, but where conditions do not allow for it; and an adopted home where they have created new lives but where social tensions and logistical hurdles have meant persistent uncertainty.

A new reality sets in

When Solomiia Pischana, a Ukrainian woman in her late twenties, fled from Kyiv to Poland in the wake of Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022, she hoped to go back that same year.

When Kyiv was secured by Ukrainian forces, a return seemed possible. In late 2022, Pischana started travelling back home to see family and friends. “I was really living between two countries. I thought a lot about going back.”

Yet quickly, a new reality set in on her visits: “In winter it became basically impossible to stay there – the constant explosions.” In Poland, by contrast, “everyone put the emphasis on helping me, on helping Ukrainians.”

In a photo essay, we look at the lives of three of the million or so Ukrainian refugees who remain in Poland one year on from Russia's invasion: Liudmyla, a mother; Vlad, an amputee soldier; and Viktoria, a high-school student https://t.co/kdOpEgt2LB

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) February 21, 2023

For many Ukrainians, Pischana’s story will feel familiar. When Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Poland became the main waystation for Ukrainians on their way out. Millions crossed the border, and while many went on to other destinations in Europe and beyond, initially more than one million remained in Poland.

The Polish state reacted quickly, assigning more than a million special identification numbers for Ukrainian refugees – known as “PESEL-UKR” – and enrolling them in the same housing and benefits systems used by Polish citizens.

So too did Polish society, with a majority of Poles working in some way to assist Ukraine or arriving refugees, and many hosting refugees in their homes.

Around 77% of Poles have been involved in helping refugees from Ukraine, for which purpose they spent around €2 billion out of their own pockets, a new study by @PIE_NET_PL has found https://t.co/xWu8JWNMui

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 28, 2022

For Ukraine, the exodus of around six million refugees meant a raft of problems. Some 650,000 military-age men left the country, while schools had to figure out how to provide remote instruction for two million children abroad.

Most of all, the refugee crisis worsened Ukraine’s demographic challenges. Before 2022, Ukraine’s population of 42 million had already been shrinking and ageing. Now, Ukraine’s minister for social policy estimates that just 22-25 million people remain in Ukrainian-controlled territory. Two thirds of Ukrainian businesses are short of workers.

Initially, many hoped for a brief war. But, as the reality of a long, grinding conflict dawned, it became clear that Ukraine could no longer plan for an imminent influx of able-bodied adults: surveys by Kyiv’s Centre for Economic Strategies show that the proportion of refugees intending to return dropped from 74% in November 2022 to 43% in January 2026.

“Rather chaotic” attempts to connect with refugees

This reality has meant that, while Ukraine needs its people back, it also knows that it cannot compel people to return to a life defined by rolling blackouts and the ever-present threat of drones and ballistic missiles.

As a result, Ukraine’s efforts to encourage and support refugee return have been haphazard and limited.

Ukraine has one deputy minister, Ilona Havronska, who is armed with just 150 million hryvnia (13.1 million zloty, €3 million) in this year’s state budget to maintain connections with refugees abroad and support their return.

Havronska has sought to create a network of “Unity Hubs,” paid for by foreign governments, where Ukrainian refugees can confer with trained consultants about returning home. Such facilities have opened in Stockholm, Prague and Berlin, with the latter receiving 5,000 visits since opening in May.

⚡️Ukraine, Germany agree to open 'Unity Hub' for Ukrainian refugees in Berlin.

"This is a professional space that brings together community, business, and cultural initiatives," National Unity Minister Oleksii Chernyshov said.https://t.co/rlTq3MpOd0

— The Kyiv Independent (@KyivIndependent) February 15, 2025

So far, however, no hub has opened in Poland, whose interior ministry told Notes from Poland: “To be frank, the Ukrainian side, Minister Havronska, they haven’t approached us much about this recently.”

Ukraine’s other major effort, a digital platform called “Dodomu” (“Homeward”), allows users to make a return plan and check off items on a digital to-do list, such as transferring medical files, verifying IDs, and registering children in Ukrainian schools.

Since launching in June, Dodomu has been used by 4,500 people in Poland, of whom 600 have completed a questionnaire about their possibility of return.

Ukraine’s efforts to reach out to refugees abroad have been “rather chaotic”, according to Olena Babakova, a Polish-Ukrainian journalist and researcher who studies migration.

 

However, a survey by the UNHCR suggests that it may not make much difference: Ukrainian refugees ranked “support for return” as less important to their decision-making than security, economic opportunities, and housing in Ukraine. Nevertheless, for older refugees and those from now-occupied territories in eastern Ukraine, large numbers cited additional information as one of their key needs.

Valentina Bryl, a Ukrainian who has lived in Poland since before 2022 and is now an HR specialist in Wrocław, notes that returning to Ukraine would mean she would have to “start everything from the beginning – my job, my life. It’s not just about safety.”

So while Bryl says that she visits Ukraine often – taking the 25-hour rail journey from Wrocław to Kharkiv to see her husband, who is serving at the front – she hasn’t made use of Dodomu or thought about the Unity Hubs. She has no intention of moving back.

From welcome to wariness in Poland

Yet for the million or so Ukrainian refugees in Poland, as well as the hundreds of thousands of Ukrainian economic migrants who came before 2022, a growing consideration is not only the conditions in Ukraine, but also the environment they face in their adopted homeland.

Poland welcomed refugees in 2022 and has supported them since. It has also benefited economically from their presence, with Ukrainian refugees estimated to have raised national GDP by 2.4% in 2025.

Ukrainian refugees boosted Poland’s GDP by 2.4% in 2025, the equivalent of €21.5bn, according to a report by the UN @Refugees agency and @Deloitte

At the same time, their growing presence in the labour market had no negative impact on employment or wages https://t.co/lcsuIwBzpy

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 8, 2026

However, there have been growing social and political tensions. During the 2025 presidential election, even liberal candidates proposed restricting child benefits for Ukrainian refugees.

The eventual winner, right-wing candidate Karol Nawrocki, in one of his first acts as president, vetoed an extension of Ukrainians’ temporary protections, before signing a revised extension that restricted benefits.

Those political changes reflect shifting attitudes in society. A June 2026 report from the Institute of Political Critique (IKP) described last year’s election campaign as a “Rubicon”, citing testimony from Ukrainian refugees that the public environment had become more hostile and historical issues had surfaced.

Pischana told Notes from Poland that, while she is “surrounded by good people” in Poland, she has noticed that “old topics like the Volhynia massacre are coming up much more”, referring to the mass slaughter of Poles by Ukrainian nationalists in World War Two. “Just walking down the street and speaking Ukrainian, it’s started to feel a bit more dangerous,” she added.

Police data show that the number of reported hate crimes against Ukrainians in Poland was 30% higher in the first half of this year than in the same period of 2025.

The number of reported hate crimes against Ukrainians in Poland is up 30% so far this year, police data show.

The figures come following recent high-profile cases of verbal and physical attacks against Ukrainians, who are Poland's largest immigrant group https://t.co/pcTsJddDz7

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 17, 2026

Myroslava Keryk, who leads Ukraiński Dom, a hub that provides services to Ukrainian refugees in Warsaw, told Notes from Poland that her staff have faced growing harassment.

She described a slew of AI-generated videos depicting them demanding Poles pay greater taxes to support refugees, as well as sexualised, fake accounts made of her employees on online apps.

Poland’s government has condemned the recent spate of hate crimes and accused the opposition and Nawrocki of stirring up such social vitriol. Meanwhile, it has begun preparing for Ukrainian refugees’ longer-term stay.

Ukrainian refugees’ current PESEL-UKR status is tied to the EU’s temporary protections, now set to expire in March 2028. So this year, the government introduced a new “CUKR” status, valid for three years of residence after it is granted. Some 75,000 Ukrainians have already submitted applications.

President Nawrocki has signed into law a government bill ending the special status granted in 2022 to Ukrainian refugees, who will now be treated on the same legal basis as other foreigners.

Nawrocki said he is "ending the era of unconditional privileges" https://t.co/BzY7wrdl49

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) February 20, 2026

This new status, however, is only a step on the path to long-term stability. CUKR, unlike most refugees’ current “UKR” status, counts toward the five years of legal stay required to apply for long-term EU resident status. However, its three-year duration means holders need to secure two additional years of legal protection in Poland before applying for long-term residency.

Polish state policies have not always made things easy for refugees. New restrictions on benefits and on travel outside of Poland have made refugees careful. Despite that, many appreciated the legal and logistical clarity of Poland’s approach, typified by the new CUKR status.

Refugees’ primary fears have concerned their social environment, not their legal status. Babakova put it neatly: “Ukrainians in Poland feel very connected to Ukrainian society, but not the state. At the same time, they have come to trust the Polish state, but not Polish society.”

The citizenship question

At the same time, a growing number of Ukrainians are thinking of obtaining citizenship, which would allow them to travel more freely and vote in Polish elections.

An August survey of Ukrainian refugees in Poland found that a plurality (35%) listed obtaining citizenship as the “most desired form of assistance” to make their lives easier.

In 2025, a record 19,000 foreigners, more than half of whom (10,000) were Ukrainian, were granted citizenship in Poland.

Poland granted citizenship to a record 19,135 foreigners in 2025, up 17% from the previous year and almost five times higher than a decade ago.

Over half of recipients were Ukrainians, followed by Belarusians, Russians, Vietnamese and Turks https://t.co/FoyWd5UPJx

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 15, 2026

But since then, Poland has moved to restrict access to citizenship – to make it “an earned privilege, not a formal certificate”, in the words of the interior ministry.

The plans include extending the required period of legal residence from five to eight years, requiring a loyalty declaration, mandating advanced knowledge of Polish, and introducing an exam on Polish history and values.

Pischana wants to become a Polish citizen: “I’ve thought that it would be logical […] I’ve lived for years in Poland. I know the language.” She added that her university thesis focuses on Polish history: she’s writing a comparison of Ukrainian and Polish songs with political or social themes, from the 1980s to the present day.

Kamil Kisiel, deputy director for the department of internal affairs and migration at Poland’s interior ministry, told Notes from Poland that the new citizenship laws, soon to be announced, will be tough: “For now, being more restrictive is the way to go, so that we can manage people’s expectations”.

The proportion of Poles who hold a negative view of relations with Ukraine has risen to the highest level ever recorded by state research agency CBOS

Meanwhile, the proportion who believe reconciliation with Ukraine is possible is at its lowest ever level https://t.co/YYBCFkVxNr

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 12, 2026

Kisiel was also up front that the Polish government does not envision many Ukrainians in Poland becoming citizens. No more than a few tens of thousands of Ukrainians have obtained Polish citizenship in the past decade, and those who arrived in 2022 are not yet eligible to apply.

Instead, Kisiel highlighted, “long-term EU residence is…the sort of stability people should expect”.

Karina, a Ukrainian woman who has been in Poland since she was 15 and did not want her surname published, says that she wants Polish citizenship as it offers “a chance to travel around the European Union, go to Spain. You can also go to America, because a Polish passport gives you visa-free travel; unfortunately, with a Ukrainian one you can’t.”

Head in Poland, heart in Ukraine

Barring a major change in the course of the war, Ukraine may even become one of the countries, including Ireland and Armenia, whose diasporas are as large or larger than their domestic population – a scenario that Havronska, the Ukrainian deputy minister, told Notes from Poland she is planning for.

At the same time, social tensions and citizenship restrictions in Poland reflect the fact that refugees are challenging Poland’s identity: since the eradication and movement of Jews, Ukrainians and Germans during and after World War Two, Poland has been a largely monoethnic nation, accustomed to one language, one faith, and one national identity. The approximately 1.5 million Ukrainians in Poland have changed that.

For Pischana, her head is in Poland while her heart remains in Ukraine, saying that she feels more attached to the culture of her homeland. “It’s a pity I can’t develop in my own country, because there’s room to do it there,” she says.

For Bryl, it’s been harder to keep close to Ukraine: “I have work, I have other responsibilities…You no longer want to read, you don’t want to get angry at some bad news”.

At the beginning, she said, she felt she had a fully Ukrainian life – just one that was put on pause. But, she adds, “when it’s already been going on for five years, and it’s still unknown how long it’ll go on, well, it’s hard to keep it on pause.”

According to prosecutors, Bartoszewski then took steps to prevent the money from being recovered. A company owned by him and his wife sold three apartments in Warsaw, after which the couple disposed of their shares in the company. His wife also donated a property to their underage children.

“As a result of these actions, Władysław Teofil Bartoszewski and his wife possess no assets from which the creditor’s claims could be satisfied,” prosecutors said.

In March 2024, a Warsaw court ordered Bartoszewski to pay the foundation more than 13.2 million zloty, plus interest. Prosecutors note that the judgment is not yet binding as an appeal is still pending.

Earlier this year, the prosecutor general, Waldemar Żurek, asked parliament to lift Bartoszewski’s immunity so that prosecutors could bring charges against him. However, he voluntarily waived it on 6 October.

At the time, Bartoszewski told newspaper Fakt that he “absolutely does not feel guilty” and “the evidence confirms this”. He also claimed that there is “a political element to my case”, though he did not elaborate further.

On Tuesday this week, prosecutors announced that they had charged Bartoszewski with misappropriation of funds of significant value – £1 million, €405,000 and 6,683,705 zloty – entrusted to him by Ciechanowiecki and the foundation. The offence carries a prison sentence of between one and 10 years.

A second charge concerns allegedly taking steps to prevent or reduce the recovery of money owed to a creditor. It carries a prison sentence of between three months and five years.

Prosecutors say that, on the same day, they “brought similar charges” against Bartoszewski’s wife and that both of the accused denied guilt.

In a statement issued later on Tuesday, Bartoszewski issued a statement rejecting the allegations and saying that he “will defend the truth and my good name in every instance, for as long as necessary”, reports the Polish Press AGency (PAP).

“I am convinced that both the criminal proceedings and the ongoing civil proceedings will confirm my arguments and rights to my property,” he added.

“I consistently maintain that all actions related to the acquisition of the real estate were consistent with the original will of Andrzej Ciechanowiecki expressed at the time of their purchase, and the premises were intended to constitute permanent financial security for my family.”

Asked whether the prime minister would dismiss Bartoszewski following the charges or wait for a court ruling, government spokesperson Adam Szłapka said that the deputy minister “is currently on leave and decisions regarding this matter will be made upon his return”.

The annual march held in Warsaw to mark Poland’s Independence Day has passed through the city without major incident. This year’s event took place amid heightened security following the deadly terrorist attack in Kraków just four days earlier.

Hundreds of thousands of people, including President Karol Nawrocki, marched through the city amid a sea of white-and-red flags. The event, which is organised by nationalist groups, also acted as a display of unity among the right-wing and far-right opposition ahead of next year’s parliamentary elections.

Figures from the more liberal government, as always, avoided the march. Prime Minister Donald Tusk celebrated Independence Day hundreds of kilometres away in the city of Szczecin, where he issued an invitation to the opposition-aligned Nawrocki to visit his home for talks.

This year’s Independence March was held under the slogan “Polak w Polsce gospodarzem”, which translates roughly as “Poles are in charge in their own country”.

The slogan was chosen to “emphasise our opposition to foreign influences on Poland and underscore that Poland should be a nation-state without mass immigration”, said Rafał Buca, the march’s spokesman. “In Poland, Poles should rule – not some foreigners, not the European Union, not big corporations.”

On the morning of the march, the organisers shared an image showing Tusk as a puppet of European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen. “Time to cut the strings of foreign influence,” they declared.

The main organisers of the march are associated with Confederation (Konfederacja), a far-right group that sits among the opposition in parliament. But it is attended by a wide range of people, from the mainstream right through to the radical right.

Leading figures from other opposition parties, including the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS), centre-right Development Plus (Rozwój Plus) and radical-right Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP), were present, as well as Nawrocki, who last year became the first Polish president to attend the march.

A member of the march’s organising committee, Marcin Osowski, told broadcaster WNET that around half a million people were at today’s event. The municipal authorities, which are under the control of Tusk’s centrist Civic Coalition (KO) party, later put the figure at around 250,000.

That would make today’s Independence March the largest ever other than the one in 2018, when a broader event was organised to mark the centenary of Poland regaining its independence after World War One.

 

The opposition was aiming to show a united front amid their ongoing protests against the recent takeover of the constitutional court by a group of government-backed judges and ahead of next year’s parliamentary elections, at which they hope to unseat Tusk’s government.

“It’s about showing our strength and, at the same time, for this march to be a springboard for the election campaign,” said Jarosław Kaczyński, leader of PIS, during the march, quoted by the Niezależna news website. “Unity is important.”

Meanwhile, one of the leaders of Confederation, Krzysztof Bosak, told the crowd in a speech that, “while we have different experiences and views, under the white-and-red flag we form one community”.

“Next year, we must turn this community into an election victory…We must remove the current clique from power and form a pro-Polish government,” he declared. “We do not accept the violent takeover of state institutions. We demand respect for the law.”

Polish defence minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz and his US counterpart, Secretary of War Pete Hegseth, have signed a statement of intent on strengthening cooperation between their defence industries.

“Today, we are taking the next steps in our alliance,” declared Hegseth, while Kosiniak-Kamysz said that the move signalled that Poland is now “not only a model ally…but has become a strategic partner of the United States”.

The Polish defence minister added that he would also push for equipment jointly manufactured by Poland and the US to be eligible for EU defence funding. “Poland is the US ambassador in the EU,” he declared.

— Ministerstwo Obrony Narodowej 🇵🇱 (@MON_GOV_PL) November 10, 2026

Kosiniak-Kamysz was welcomed by Hegseth in Washington to discuss a range of issues relating to security cooperation. A major item on the agenda was Poland’s desire for a new permanent US military base on its territory.

After the meeting, Kosiniak-Kamysz told reporters that there was a “green light from the Pentagon” for the base, with the final decision now resting with the White House. He said that was expected to be made in early December.

Hegseth, meanwhile, praised Poland for embracing the “NATO 3.0” concept, under which the US wants Europe to take on more responsibility for its own defence.

“Poland is building one of the most formidable armies in Europe, ready to secure and defend its territory,” said the Secretary of War, who noted that Warsaw is “leading by example” with its high levels of defence spending.

 

Hegseth also welcomed the fact that Poland is investing significantly in US equipment, including Abrams tanks, F-35 fighter jets, Apache helicopters and Patriot air-defence systems.

“You are building a fully modernised, interoperable force, and our two nations are…giving military cooperation industrial depth as well,” said the secretary of war.

Hegseth also reaffirmed Washington’s desire for a peace deal in Ukraine and “encouraged Kosiniak-Kamysz to continue Poland’s steadfast support of Ukraine”, said Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell.

American defense technology is driving innovation and creating new opportunities for transatlantic industrial cooperation.@USAmbNATO Matthew Whitaker, Assistant Secretary of Commerce David Fogel @CommerceGov and @USAmbPoland Tom Rose met with Deputy Minister of Defence… pic.twitter.com/5etw1L3X5A

Kosiniak-Kamysz said that the statement of intent he had signed with Hegseth was aimed at ensuring more US equipment was manufactured and maintained in Poland itself, including technology transfers.

He also said that he wants to secure European funds for jointly produced US equipment. The EU’s SAFE programme of defence loans, for example, largely excludes US manufacturers.

“We want American equipment manufactured by Polish-American companies to benefit from European funding. I will present such a position next Tuesday at the meeting of EU defence ministers,” said Kosiniak-Kamysz. “Poland is the US ambassador to the EU.”

The meeting between the two defence secretaries also coincided with the Transatlantic Defence Industry Access Forum, which brought together 70 Polish and 80 American firms, with the aim of strengthening ties between the two countries’ defence industries.

W ostatnich dniach dobra decyzja o utworzeniu w Polsce centrum serwisowego rakiet Patriot, a dziś podpisaliśmy kolejne porozumienie z USA, które przyspieszy współpracę naszych przemysłów zbrojeniowych.
