Last month, the United States chose Poland as the location for a planned facility for servicing and maintaining Patriot missiles – the first to be located outside the US itself.

In July, it was announced that Polish state defence group PGZ would become the first European producer of American Barracuda-500M cruise missiles. In May, an agreement was signed to establish a centre in Poland for servicing the engines of Abrams tanks.

That same month, President Donald Trump announced that his country would station an additional 5,000 troops in Poland, prompting Warsaw to formally request the establishment of a new US military base, which President Karol Nawrocki has suggested should be called “Fort Trump”.

City AM https://www.cityam.com/ London's Business Newspaper Mon, 16 Nov 2026 19:03:57 +0000 en-GB hourly 1 https://wordpress.org/?v=7.1.4 https://www.cityam.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/09/app_launcher_icon_final_rounded.png?w=32 City AM https://www.cityam.com/ 32 32 213406410 ‘Complete system reset’: Burnham urged to find ‘political will’ for Milburn’s welfare overhaul https://www.cityam.com/complete-system-reset-burnham-urged-to-find-political-will-for-milburns-welfare-overhaul/ Mon, 16 Nov 2026 22:30:00 +0000 https://www.cityam.com/?p=2478258

Andy Burnham will need to “summon the resources and political will” to deliver the youth unemployment tsar Alan Milburn’s proposals to cut benefits and boost investment in employment, industry figures have said.  Milburn is set to publish a lengthy plan featuring calls for extensive welfare reform – including employment subsidies – in a bid to [...]]]>

Andy Burnham will need to “summon the resources and political will” to deliver the youth unemployment tsar Alan Milburn’s proposals to cut benefits and boost investment in employment, industry figures have said. 

Milburn is set to publish a lengthy plan featuring calls for extensive welfare reform – including employment subsidies – in a bid to bring nearly 1m young people currently out of employment, education or training (Neets) into the national workforce. 

In a speech on Tuesday morning, the former Blair-era health secretary will argue that “half measures will not do” and that a “complete system reset is needed”, posing a political test for Labour parliamentarians who are disgruntled by the prospect of cuts to benefits.

Milburn is set to argue against “crude cuts” with a warning that savings in the welfare bill could take years to materialise.

“A lost generation is not a fact of life, it is a choice, and I believe it is the wrong one,” Milburn is expected to say. 

“Not just because it is a fiscal crisis or an economic crisis, but because it is a moral one.   

He will add: “It is time for a new settlement that makes work not welfare the future for the next generation.”  

Burnham’s policies ‘must flow’ from Milburn’s review

Ahead of his report’s launch, industry chiefs, who offered input into the review taking place over the last 12 months, described proposals as “ambitious” as they urged Burnham to adopt proposals even as a growing number of Labour MPs have expressed concerns. 

Andy Haldane, the former Bank of England chief economist who advised Burnham during his Makerfield by-election campaign, said there was “no more pressing challenge” in the country than reducing the number of Neets. 

“Milburn’s report provides the blueprint for doing so. It is now for the government to summon the resources and political will to deliver on that blueprint,” Haldane said. 

Tina McKenzie, the chair of the industry body representing small businesses, said helping employers with business costs and increasing young entrepreneurship would be “vital for social mobility”.

“Bringing forward support for young people who have been economically inactive for too long and giving them a genuine chance to gain experience and build confidence, is an important step and small businesses are well placed as long as public policy decisions now flow from the review,” she said. 

Some of the Labour backbenchers to criticise Milburn’s proposals include Bell Ribeiro-Addy and Clive Lewis, who publicly backed Burnham’s return to parliament during Sir Keir Starmer’s premiership. 

Proposals in Milburn’s review include a full reform of the benefits system, increasing the number of apprenticeships, expanding access to mental health support and subsidies for employers taking on risks by hiring young people.  

‘Decade’ before savings come

An interim review earlier this year found that for every £1 the government invested in employment, about £25 was spent on benefits. An addition of the costs of the Neets crisis for the UK economy came to around £125bn every year. 

Under Milburn’s plans, mayors will be accountable for delivery through agreements while a new ‘Youth Opportunity Service’ would be created around the country. The service will connect young people to advisers, who will set up career plans. 

Milburn previously cautioned that, as a result of up-front investment, savings could take about a decade to emerge. 

He said his proposals formed the basis of a national ambition to bring the Neets rate from 13 per cent down to around five per cent by 2036. 

Pat McFadden, the work and pensions secretary, is set to respond to the full report on Tuesday afternoon.

Shadow work and pensions secretary Helen Whately said the review was “too cautious on reversing” damage done by higher taxes and more regulation imposed on businesses.

“Overall, it fails to bring down the welfare bill, proposes billions more in government spending and won’t make the slightest difference for young people stuck on welfare now – because nothing will happen for at least three years,” Whately said.

The City’s new lord mayor will use his first set-piece speech to call on Britain’s pension funds to speed up efforts to homegrown start-ups and scale-ups.

In an eagerly anticipated speech on Monday, former Hiscox chief Bronek Masojada will lament the lack of institutional cash made available for fast-growing businesses and infrastructure projects, warning the pattern is harming savers, businesses and the UK economy.

“It is the paradox of our time that Britain has one of the world’s largest pools of domestic capital whilst having a shortage of domestic capital for scale-up and infrastructure opportunities,” he is expected to say. “This is especially so when UK private capital data shows that private assets have delivered a rate of return of 12.4 per cent after fees over the past 20 years.”

The intervention is Masojada’s first as the City of London’s 698th lord mayor, after he was fast-tracked to the plumb civic and ambassadorial role.

Pension funds slow to ramp up private market functions

The South African-born insurance heavyweight was given just a few hours’ notice to accept the offer , following frontrunner Tim Hailes’ abrupt decision to withdraw amid criminal proceedings being launched against his former business partner.

Masojada was officially sworn in on Friday, and processed through the streets of the City as part of the lord mayor’s show the following day.

Speaking at a banquet to mark his appointment, the Square Mile’s new political figurehead will challenge pension funds to justify why they are not offering a more full-throated backing to UK growth-stage firms.

“Foreign capital doesn’t have this problem,” he is expected to say. “Canadian and Australian pension funds invest over seven times more in infrastructure than our defined contribution industry. Our scale up companies are funded by British based private equity firms, but the majority of their capital comes from overseas.

“What is that this foreign capital sees that we do not?”

Robert Pattinson will be a great Bond – but his casting is bad news for Hollywood

In new stills released today it has been announced that Twilight and Batman actor Robert Pattinson will be the seventh actor to officially drink freezing cold vodka and a tiny bit of vermouth to play orphaned, traumatised, fashionable, perennially middle-aged James Bond.  

Pattinson, who is 40 and rose to prominence through the five filmic adaptations of the Twilight Saga books, is a good choice. Firstly, he is a fine actor, with a range of indie projects under his belt, and an undefinable, hard-to-read quality that makes him alluring to Hollywood. You couldn’t quite pinpoint where he hangs out – the pub, a fine pile in the Hollywood Hills or a grungy gig – and it is that indie-to-mainstream crossover appeal has helped him sustain a career this long, developing the sort of CV former 007 producer Barbara Broccoli prefers (Daniel Craig, too, had been an indie darling before he picked up the holster). 

If you were to rank his undefinable, draw-you-in qualities, those smokey eyes that somehow seem both blue and brown but give nothing away would be at the top of the list.

Robert Pattinson is good for James Bond, bad for Hollywood

But Pattinson’s casting is less good for Hollywood. James Bond is surely the last role that could rocket an unheard of actor to the A-List, and not casting a burgeoning name is a missed opportunity. 

These days, it is incredibly hard to birth new stars. It was not this way in the 1990s when Pierce Brosnan was cast, and to some extent with Daniel Craig. Back then, putting a new face on the cover of The Sunday Times Culture magazine could make someone famous. I recall the former editor of that magazine telling me he’d once argued to give the cover to a little-known actor called Tom Cruise, and we all know how that went. But journalism doesn’t have a tenth of that power anymore – put someone on the front of a weekend supplement and they might generate a few hundred Instagram followers, but not a glittering Blockbuster career.

And then there are the nepo babies – the Anais Gallaghers, Hero Fiennes Tiffins and Rafferty Laws – clogging up the talent pipeline, making it even harder for new actors who don’t have famous parents to break through. 

The cinema also used to be a good platform for rising actors, but with fewer people going to the flicks at the weekend, and fewer films being made, producers are choosing safety by relying on bankable stars rather than newcomers (hello, R Patz). The death of the rom-com is a signifier of how people are mostly going to the cinema to see ‘event’ films these days, like new Batman, Spider-Man or James Bond films.

The power of franchises at the box office was proven again recently when Tom Cruise’s latest film, Digger, became one of the biggest box office disasters of the decade. Cruise’s casting alone couldn’t drum up interest from the public, illustrating how big stars can’t always guarantee box office return without the weight of franchises like Mission Impossible behind them.

One man who can, though, is James Bond. Ian Fleming’s spy could remedy all of these problems: I’ll put it simply: cast anyone to play him, and the cinemas will sell out.

I mean, not literally anyone, but cast someone good, and people will go. 

This clearly doesn’t play into the interests of new Bond owners Amazon – they just want a big name because a big name sells, especially after investing £1bn in new Pinewood studio expansion – but it would be good for the pipeline of cinema.

Creating an exciting new star is high-on impossible these days – and Bond choosing not to take a punt on an upcoming name is a shame for Hollywood.

Poundland-owner Gordon Brothers has attracted fierce criticism in recent weeks over its attempted sale of the discount retailer. Felix Armstrong asks: who are the owners and what do they want?

To Liam Byrne, chair of Parliament’s business select committee, Gordon Brothers is “like a wolf on Wall Street, ravaging the British high street”. In its own words, the Boston-based investment firm is a “leading global asset expert”, which “helps companies move forward through change”. 

Few companies have endured more change in recent months than Poundland, the ubiquitous high street chain which is staring down the barrel of collapse little more than a year after Gordon Brothers snapped it up for a token £1. 

The investment firm, and its European head Mark Newton-Jones, were thrust into the public eye last week when Byrne and his fellow committee members hauled the Poundland owner into Parliament to answer for its handling of the retailer’s sale. 

The group’s refusal of solvent offers for Poundland has attracted the condemnation of political figures and retail bosses. Andy Burnham has called on Gordon Brothers to explain why it has not found a deal for the group, while Reform UK treasury spokesperson Robert Jenrick has dubbed the group a “corporate raider”. 

Lord Richard Walker, the executive chairman of Iceland, which is eyeing Poundland stores in the event that it is broken up, told City AM that “something very whiffy has gone on” during Gordon Brothers’ ownership of the retailer.

“I think it’s more about private equity opportunism because the figures [suggest] Poundland was trading okay, actually. So I don’t like the smell of it and it’s right that politicians have stepped in to question it,” he said.

Though Gordon Brothers has only recently become the subject of public anger, it has a long history of liquidating distressed British brands. When it was founded in Boston in 1903, the firm specialised in generating cash from the stock of retailers which were going bust. 

More recently the group has invested in a string of struggling high street companies, including video rental Blockbuster, clothes retailer Laura Ashley and women’s luxury fashion brand LK Bennett.

Gordon Brothers tapped former Mothercare boss Newton-Jones in February 2023 to head up its Europe, Middle East and Asian operations. During his time as chief executive of the maternity products retailer, he “led [its] turnaround and restructure toward a profitable global business,” his profile on the company’s website reads.

Newton-Jones’s former board members would give a more mixed account of his time at the firm. He became known as Mothercare’s “boomerang” boss after the group’s board re-hired him just 36 days after his unceremonious departure – or “forced sabbatical,” as he has described it.

Just 18 months after his reappointment, Mothercare collapsed into administration. The group, which employed 2,800 people at the time, had been “hit hard by increasing cost pressures and changes in consumer spending,” administrators said.

‘Strangled of access to funds’

When Poundland narrowly avoided collapse in June 2025, few of its 12,000 employees would have predicted that their jobs would be back on the chopping block before the next year was out. 

Gordon Brothers beat out rivals including Modella Capital, Hilco Capital and Endless to snap up the retailer from PepCo, its previous owner. Gordon Brothers’s restructuring plan, which forced the closure of more than 150 stores and the loss of about 2,200 jobs, was approved by a judge who ruled that the company would have fallen into administration without it.

Gordon Brothers has faced fierce criticism for stripping £18m in proceeds from Poundland in its 16-month stewardship of the company. The investment firm appointed advisers for a sale process in September, which was thrust into the spotlight after it refused a bid from Irish firm Martin Property Group in a row over how much of a £30m loan it was willing to cover.

Poundland’s directors filed a notice to appoint administrators in late October, setting a 10-day deadline – which has since been extended – for it to find a new home. Xyra Group and Innovest Holdings have since emerged as competitors to Martin Property Group with bids for the whole company, but it is feared the business is barrelling towards an administration which would see its stores flogged to rival retailers.

As Poundland awaits its future, Gordon Brothers has been accused of blocking it from accessing funds needed to keep its shelves stocked since the sale process began last month. 

Byrne said last week that he has seen evidence the retailer was “being strangled of access to its own funds,” though people close to Gordon Brothers blamed Poundland’s notice to appoint administrators, which they said makes it more complicated to approve the release of cash.

Gordon Brothers released two payments – of £10.3m and £10.9m – to Poundland on Tuesday and Thursday last week and is set to release a larger sum next week to cover payroll for the retailer’s thousands of employees, people close to the process said.

These actions have not stopped the investment firm facing accusations that it is barrelling the retailer towards collapse. MPs present at the Parliament hearing last week said it was “abundantly clear” that Gordon Brothers would make more money if it flogged Poundland’s stores and stock to separate buyers, rather than finding a buyer for the firm as a whole.

Poundland’s ‘model is challenged’

Jonas Lind Clement, whose company Florelle supplies artificial plants to Poundland, told City AM it is “appalling that Gordon Brothers are not taking up the offers they have on the table”. The retailer’s collapse could have a “devastating” effect on the 30,000 jobs in its supply chain, they added.

Steve Smith, who founded Poundland with the help of his father in 1990, believes the retailer deserves to stay on British high streets because it draws shoppers into town centres and challenges its competitors to cut its prices.

He told City AM: “Competition is good. It keeps other retailers sharp and it keeps prices low. If people like Poundland start going, you’re going to find all the prices will go through the roof, and the public will be worse off.” 

Gordon Brothers believes no business has an inherent right to be on the high street, people close to the firm said. One pointed to the exit of the majority of the 80 parties who had initially expressed an interest in the company, leaving only three.

The company said: “The market spoke, and the market said: ‘We don’t think this business in its current form is sustainable. We think the model is challenged, and we think actually there is still value in Poundland, but it is better being broken up and being absorbed by other existing retailers.’”

Gordon Brothers’ insistence that Poundland remains in a “vulnerable” position appeared to be undermined by reports that it posted an £18m profit in the year to September, bouncing back from a £68m loss in the year before.

But sources close to the sale suggested that, based on the £1.5bn revenue the retailer generated last year, this profit would represent a margin of little more than one per cent.

In the coming years, low-margin retailers “will evolve and probably be bought by and be absorbed by retailers that are doing better and are able to,” the person close to Gordon Brothers said. “It’s not the case that the high street is dead, it’s just evolving.”

Gordon Brothers declined to comment. A spokesperson for the group said last week: “While our preference remains a sale of the whole company, we are taking due care to ensure that any successful offer can provide the funds required to acquire the business and see it through to sustainable cash generation. 

“We, the board, and all involved are working to secure a credible plan that delivers certainty, preserves value and protects as many jobs as possible.”

António Simões always knew he had big shoes to fill at Legal & General.

The Portuguese former banker took over from Sir Nigel Wilson in 2024, succeeding an 11-year tenure which saw the chief executive receive a knighthood.

Wilson championed regulatory reform that would free insurance and pension funds to back long-term infrastructure projects around the UK, but the end of his reign was overshadowed by the turmoil that gripped pension funds in September 2022, when Liz Truss’ disastrous ‘mini Budget’ sparked a sell-off in gilt markets.

When Simões arrived in January 2024 and conducted his six-month review into the business, the fallout was no longer an emergency, but had reshaped the UK pension landscape.

This left Simões to wield the axe over the firm to turn it into a “leaner operation”, including sharpening its pension arm and reducing the group’s four businesses to three by merging its asset management divisions.

Shares have increased 17.9 per cent since January to 309.4p, but its latest update on Monday knocked the stock back two per cent, as investors questioned whether the plan is still on track.

Pivot to private

Simões who previously worked for Santander and HSBC, had the merger of the firm’s investment management and private capital arm at the heart of his plans.

The FTSE 100 giant is shifting away from low-margin passive index funds and into higher-fee private credit, real estate and infrastructure, and vowed to keep increasing investment over the next two years.

On paper, the strategy is ahead of schedule, after Simões outlined guidance to grow private market assets under management from £48bn to £85bn by 2028. By the half-year mark in August 2026, total private markets AUM had already rocketed to £79bn.

L&G’s workplace pensions also arm pulled in £8bn of net inflows in the first nine months of the year, a 57 per cent increase, with £4.5bn in the third quarter alone, driven by deals signed in the period including one with Royal Mail.

“Workplace was the standout performer,” said Richard Hunter, head of markets at Interactive Investor.

“This is vindication for the moment of the group’s broad retail proposition, with demand clearly in evidence.”

But despite the rush out of passive funds, the insurance giant saw investors remove £28bn from its asset management arm in the first nine months of the year, more than triple the £8bn drawn the prior year.

Although the pace of withdrawals slowed to £3bn in the latest financial period, coupled with negative market movements, £12bn was wiped off L&G’s AUM, reaffirming the growth is not yet enough to stem heavy outflows from its traditional channels.

Margins over market share

Simões has also orchestrated a major overhaul of L&G’s bulk purchase annuity sales and pension risk transfer (PRT) market.

The insurer is shifting away from chasing deal volumes, instead focusing on higher-margin buyouts while also converting its existing investment clients into annuity customers.

Bulk annuity volumes increased 54 per cent year on year in the third quarter to £3.7bn. L&G has also written or agreed exclusive terms of £6.7bn in PRT transactions this year to date, with £6.2bn in the UK.

But L&G faces a steep climb to meet its target of writing between £50bn and £65bn of UK pension transfers by 2028. 

Since 2024, the group has written or agreed terms on £25bn in the UK, leaving it at risk of not meeting its goal in two years.

Shareholders were also left unimpressed by flat PRT and high net asset management outflows, causing its stock to fall.

“Legal & General may have boosted its full-year earnings guidance but there were enough minor disappointments in its third quarter update to put the shares on the back foot,” said Russ Mould, investment director at AJ Bell. 

“The volume of completed pension risk transfer deals underwhelmed, coming in lower year-on-year.”

Trimming the company

Simões has also taken aim at the company’s payroll, doing away with overlapping management across its divisions and removing roles which have driven up back-office costs.

The group confirmed it had launched a mass job cut programme in September, which will see 1,000 roles cut by mid next year, representing roughly 10 per cent of its workforce.

“Over the last decade, different structures, processes and ways of working have developed across L&G, making us more complex than we need to be,” Simões told staff in an email in September.

“To deliver our strategy successfully… across L&G, we need to change how we work today and, through this, become a leaner organisation.”

Higher investment returns and trading across the firm, have helped keep full-year core operating earnings on track to beat the top end of L&G’s 6 to 9 per cent growth target.

“We believe L&G’s shares continue to be underpinned by an attractive basic cash yield… the remaining portion of the £1.2bn share buyback will continue to support the shares,” analysts at Peel Hunt said.

“Back in 2024, I set out a strategy to grow L&G as a simpler, better-connected business,” said Simões in the group’s latest quarterly update.

“Three years on, we are on track to meet or exceed all our targets. We are also improving how we serve our customers, and changing how we work to give us a more efficient platform for the next phase of growth.”

For now, Simões has proved he can strip out costs and protect L&G’s prized dividend, but until its fund outflows slow and pension deals pick up pace, the turnaround remains only half done.

The yield on the two-year gilt climbed four basis points on Monday, passing the symbolic five per cent milestone after a string of hawkish remarks from key monetary policy rate-setters.

The sell-off, which swept up both long and short duration bonds, extends a run of declines that last week saw gilts suffer their worst week in three months.

Two-year gilt yields have risen more than 30 basis points (bps) – or a third of a percentage point – since Tuesday, as hopes of an immediate ceasefire in the wake of the US midterms faded. The yield on the UK’s 10-year government bonds, which reflect sentiment toward a country’s fiscal and inflation outlook, has climbed 25 bps.

Traders now attribute an 84 per cent chance to the Bank’s Monetary Policy Committee voting for a second consecutive interest rate rise when it meets next month. They have fully priced in a third rate hike by March, and believe there is an 84 per cent chance of a fourth vote to tighten policy by the end of April.

That would leave so-called Bank Rate as high as 4.75 per cent just months into 2027, in what would constitute the monetary’s authority’s second major rate hiking cycle in less than four five years.

Chief economist Huw Pill, who is seen as one of the most hawkish members of the Bank’s nine-strong rate-setting committee, warned on Saturday there would likely need to be an interest rate hike either side of the new year to extinguish rising inflation.

“We have further to go,” he told the Financial Times on Saturday, adding that the Bank “waited too long” before hiking central borrowing costs earlier this month.

His remarks were echoed by fellow rate-setter Megan Greene, who said proactively taming inflation through rate hikes was also her preferred option.

“I think the risk ​of not getting on top of inflation coming out of a period when we’ve had inflation ‌over ⁠target for the best part of about five-and-a-half years, that’s the bigger risk, that would be the bigger policy mistake,” she said. “So I think there’s a benefit in acting proactively in terms of kind of screwing it up the least.”

Earlier this month, the MPC voted to raise interest rates for the first time in three years, fearful that the energy shock from the ongoing Middle East conflict is poised to spread into the wider UK economy.

In the eight months since the start of the war, there has been little evidence of so-called second-round effects, whereby businesses pass their rising costs onto consumers and workers ask for higher pay packets. But a string of strong economic data releases – and signs of a recovery in the labour market – has put rate-setters on high alert.

In a letter to the City regulator’s chief, Griffith said proposals to force listed companies to report on sustainability would hamper Britain’s capital markets and dampen IPO prospects in London. 

He pointed to advice from the Listing Authority Advisory Panel, a body at the FCA that advises the regulator on policy affecting markets, that said new environmental, social and governance rules for listed companies would leave the UK “out of step” with international peers. 

The LAAP also noted that sustainability disclosures were a “widely cited frustration among listed companies”. 

The new “comply or explain” rules, which are due to come into effect next year, will require listed companies to either adhere to governance codes or justify departures from it. 

Griffith said ESG and climate-related reporting requirements “impose billions of pounds of costs on businesses for little to no benefit”. He said the FCA should “refrain from introducing these new regulatory requirements”.

President Donald Trump has backed calls to reinstate Jensen Huang as chief executive of Nvidia, as the chipmaker’s shares fell more than two per cent upon Wall Street open on Monday, extending last week’s bruising losses.

The AI heavyweight slipped 2.7 per cent to $158.7 (£120.3) in early trading, as investors came to grips with the fallout of Jensen Huang’s departure from the firm after 33 years and subsequent rumours that he is mulling a comeback. 

The founder and chief executive resigned last Thursday, following reports of multiple extramarital affairs, including one with a woman who is suspected of being a Chinese spy by US intelligence officials and Nvidia’s vice president of healthcare. 

Trump joined a chorus of tech executives who have called for his reinstatement, including SpaceX founder Elon Musk, and downplayed national security concerns about the ousted executive’s relationship with the suspected spy.

“I would not mind that”, Trump told reporters on Monday.

“A lot of people are asking Jensen, they think Jensen should go back. That certainly isn’t a bad idea.”

But this position has put Trump at odds with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who called for a “dramatic shakeup” in Nvidia and called for an external search for new leadership.

Monday’s decline followed Nvidia’s Friday losses, where the company shed two per cent, closing the session at $162.8 per share.

But it was Thursday which led the week for Nvidia’s most volatile session, after shares plunged more than 13 per cent at the opening bell before recovering to close just over four per cent lower.

Waiting for Tuesday’s closing bell

The stock has fallen 32 per cent from its October peak and has seen hundreds of billions be wiped off its market cap. The chipmaker is set to release its latest quarterly results on 17 November.

The scandal has raised questions over Nvidia’s leadership and corporate governance, with chief financial officer Colette Kress taking over as interim chief executive while the board searches for a permanent successor.

Patrick Munnelly, market strategist at Tickmill group, said: “The AI ecosystem faces a twin public and private stress test this week.  Tomorrow’s Nvidia earnings print takes on monumental significance following Jensen Huang’s abrupt resignation.

“Interim chief executive Colette Kress must deliver airtight forward guidance, roadmap continuity, and customer assurances to stem multiple compression across the semiconductor supply chain.”

But a number of equity analysts have downgraded Nvidia with CLSA the latest to change its rating, dropping it to Outperform and slashing its price target from $425 to $225.

Wider losses and shareholder woes

US markets opened mixed on Monday, with the S&P 500 sliding 0.8 per cent, while the Dow Jones industrial Average inched down 0.2 per cent.

The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite Index fell 2.1 per cent, as selling pressure plagues fellow chipmaker stocks. 

Nvidia’s rival AMD and Broadcom shed 5.1 per cent and 4.2 per cent respectively.

Meanwhile, Intel shed 5.7 per cent, with the heavy losses reversing all three firm’s gains from last week. Intel’s losses were deepened by it being sued by shareholders, who accused the firm of hiding the severity of a slump in PC sales that caused its share price to plunge nearly 29 per cent in one day and knocking billions of its value.

The latest sell-off also seeped into Asia, as South Korea’s blue-chip index sunk 3.5 per cent. Losses were led by tech heavyweights Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix, which fell 4.4 per cent and 7.8 per cent respectively.

Japan’s Nikkei 225 slipped 2.4 per cent, with the index shedding 8.6 per cent in the last month.

The anti-fraud agency has charged eight individuals in connection with the collapse of London Capital & Finance (LCF) following a £237m Ponzi scheme.

The Serious Fraud Office (SFO) has charged Michael Andrew Thomson (53), Simon Hume-Kendall (73), Elten Barker (53), Paul Careless (51), Robert Sedgwick (78) and John Russell-Murphy (52) with conspiracy to defraud. Helen Hume-Kendall (64) was charged with concealing criminal property.

An eighth defendant has been charged with conspiracy to defraud and acting in contravention of a director disqualification undertaking. It is understood that this individual’s legal team will apply for anonymity at the first magistrates’ court hearing.

The investment company collapsed in January 2019 after the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) intervened after discovering it was marketing unregulated mini-bonds and making misleading promises of returns. LCF sold around 16,000 bonds to around 11,600 bondholders, totalling over £237m.

All eight defendants are due to appear before Westminster Magistrates’ Court on 7 December.

Emma Isaac, head of division for the Serious Fraud Office, said: “Thousands of investors believed backing London Capital & Finance would yield high returns, instead they lost over £250m. Today’s charges mark a significant step forward in our investigation into the collapse of the firm and ensuring those responsible are held to account.”

High Court Ponzi ruling

Evelyn Partners, the administrators for collapsed LCF, launched the civil lawsuit in 2020 against the company’s former executives. The original claim was against 15 defendants but before the hearing six defendants reached settlements.

The trial went ahead in February 2024 against Michael Thomson, Spencer Golding, Paul Careless, John Russell-Murphy, Robert Sedgwick, Surge Financial, and Grosvenor Park Intelligent Investment. However, during the 20-week trial, Golding was disbarred from defending himself.

In November that year, Mr Justice Miles handed down his 341-page judgment, concluding that the investment company engaged in fraudulent business practices.

Following the ruling, the High Court informed Golding, Thomson, Russell-Murphy and Sedgwick that they were liable for £180m in the civil lawsuit. The court ruled that former police officer Careless was liable for 75 per cent of that figure in the high-profile scandal. Careless and Russell-Murphy were also found liable for a dishonest assistance claim of £211m.

There’s been much speculation about AI’s impact on the employment market. Predictions vary across a wide spectrum, from the anti-luddite “AI will displace jobs, not replace them” approach all the way to the Elon Musk-style “work will soon be optional” thesis.

So far, there is very little hard data available to furnish the more alarmist views. According to the latest data, while at 4.7 per cent the current level of UK unemployment is well above the sub-four per cent post-pandemic lows, the rate remains below the 21st century average of 5.4 per cent.

Last month, City AM analysed news reports of mass UK layoffs over the past two years, spanning more than 130,000 roles. The companies behind the cuts were much more likely to attribute the layoffs to higher costs, including rising taxes, than they were to automation.

Ben Caswell, senior economist at the National Institute of Economic and Social Research, says there is no “smoking gun evidence” that AI had been a major cause of the steady rise in unemployment and decline in vacancies in the UK, which were “quite broad-based.”

That being said, in some parts of the economy the effect of AI on the labour market is becoming more pronounced.

Among the first victims to the technology has been call centre jobs, which are rapidly on the decline. Sky, for instance, last year said it would cut as many as 2,000 call centre jobs last year as part of a shift to “digital self-service.”

There has also been a sharp drop in hiring at professional services firms like PwC and Deloitte, though arguably some of this can be put down to pandemic-era overhiring.

But there is one part of the economy rapidly where AI’s advance is becoming clear: financial services.

Banks, insurance firms and pension funds are shedding jobs at speed. To name a few: HSBC has cut more than four thousand (the medium-term target could be as high as twenty thousand), Barclays is cutting five thousand, Standard Chartered more than seven thousand.

L&G has cemented its position on the league table today, confirming earlier reports that it has set into motion a plan to axe 1,000 roles.

“We continue to take action to make L&G simpler, more efficient and more competitive, building on the progress we have made since 2024,” the FTSE 100 firm said this morning.

“As part of this programme, we commenced a staff redundancy exercise in September, with broader organisational changes expected to result in a reduction of around 1,000 roles by the middle of next year.”

Crucially, many cuts in the sector relate to the premium end of services such as wealth management, as much as they do bank branches and call centres. According to a report last month, HSBC plans to axe as many as 70 per cent of financial advisers within its wealth management arm.

This presents a key test for financial services: can they keep charging premium fees to top clients without offering the same level of human-led service? Will clients pay through the nose for AI-led advisory services when, with a bit of training, they could get ninety percent of the job done with a £20 Claude subscription? Banks seem to think so.

The ‘mansion tax’ is pure extortion and inspectors should not be able to take photographs of your home to abet what amounts to theft, says Charles Amos

Whitehall instructions for mansion tax inspectors to photograph homes without owners’ consent are a gross invasion of privacy. No tax inspector has a right to take photos for the purposes of enforcing the mansion tax because the mansion tax itself is pure extortion: It is nothing but a revenue raising exercise to further soak the productive parts of the country, i.e. London and the south east. Yet again Labour are demonstrating they have no regard for private property; not even in that most tender area of our lives – our own homes.

Taxation only has two good justifications: helping the truly destitute and protecting people against foreign invaders and domestic criminals. The state’s budget is already £1.4 trillion, more than enough to finance the two purposes mentioned, meaning, the £430m to be raised from the mansion tax amounts to pure extortion of the rich. Taking £2,500 from a £2m homeowner in Chelsea via the mansion tax to fund leisure centres, bus shelters and libraries in Hartlepool is theft: We’d never accept a private person taking that money for such purposes because the need is not serious enough in any of the three cases, nor should the state. Certainly, when the state is funding £145bn of working age and child welfare this should be redirected to any essential needs local councils might still have first before raising yet more tax. 

Even if you don’t get on board with this libertarian argument though, surely, it must be agreed people should pull their own weight. The local government secretary, Steve Reed, says it’s unjust that a £10m Band H house in Mayfair pays £2,100 in council tax currently while a £400,000 Band D house in Blackpool pays £2,500. Yet the rich householder in Mayfair justly pays less than the poorer householder of Blackpool because the Londoner uses fewer services and the Blackpooler far more. Plus: Some council tax is much lower because the councils are run a lot better, such as Wandsworth. Reed should not simply look at lower figures and punish residents with higher taxes which might well just amount to a surcharge for efficiency! 

Burglary

Now we have established the mansion tax is pure extortion we can see why taking photos of people’s homes is wrong. An analogy helps. If burglars were taking photos of homes deliberately so they could size them up to only break into the most plentifully stocked, then we’d be quite right in taking their cameras and smashing them to pieces. Although taking pictures of people’s homes is not per se wrong, where doing so is part of an unjust scheme it becomes wrong too. Tax inspectors taking pictures of people’s homes to present them with a massive bill and then threaten them with jail for nonpayment are taking part in an unjust scheme, so, their photography becomes wrongful. If an invasion of privacy is taken to include taking photos you’ve no right to take, then tax inspectors invade privacy. 

Steve Reed will, of course, dispute the very foundation of my argument. As a Labour politician who believes in some form of egalitarianism, he has no ultimate concern for private property, or, indeed, home ownership, because both stand in the way of equality. Along with Sir Edward Coke, I say: “An Englishman’s home is his castle’. It doesn’t matter how you’ve justly acquired it, via luck or hard work, it should be a sacred place which goes entirely undisturbed. Your home is your own and Labour ought to stay out of it. And not photograph it either.

Charles Amos writes The Musing Individualist Substack

With an array of high-performance hypercars already on sale, standing out is a challenge. However, Holland-based Sanrivatti has discovered a unique angle with the One.

The car features what Sanrivatti calls its ‘Apex Position’ inside. This places the driver head-first in the cockpit, seated as if they were riding a superbike.

Designed for one person only, the Sanrivatti One uses a carbon fibre monocoque chassis, which helps reduce its kerb weight to just 1,100kg.

A mid-mounted V10 engine, motorsport-style pushrod suspension, AP Racing brakes and Michelin slick tyres all point towards a focus on high-speed track driving.

Why the Sanrivatti One puts its driver head-first

Although there are still many unanswered questions around how the Apex Position will work, including whether the One has a conventional steering wheel, there is method behind Sanrivatti’s apparent madness.

Testing in digital and physical simulators showed the head-forward Apex Position gave drivers an average of 3.2 times more visible racing surface through turn three at Silverstone when compared to 10 benchmark hypercars.

An 800hp naturally aspirated V10

A Judd-designed 5.5-litre V10 engine serves up a monstrous 800hp and 516lb ft of torque. The naturally aspirated motor revs to 9,000rpm, and is mated to a six-speed Hewland sequential transmission.

A power-to-weight ratio of 727hp per tonne should provide the Dutch hypercar with explosive performance, including a top speed of 205mph.

John W Judd, managing director at Judd Engines, said: “A naturally aspirated V10 is about far more than the headline power figure. Of equal importance is the way an engine responds, builds through its rev range and connects the driver’s inputs to the performance of the car.”

Sanrivatti One design: Falcon meets fighter jet

The exterior shape of the One, led by designer Robin van Tilborg, takes inspiration from both a peregrine falcon and a modern fighter jet. The one-piece canopy roof is integrated directly into the bodywork, rather than sitting above it.

Santiago Sanchez Rivero, founder and CEO of Sanrivatti, said: “When we started Sanrivatti, we didn’t want to create another hypercar that simply followed the established formula with more power and more technology. We wanted to question something more fundamental: what it actually feels like to drive.

“The One is the first time people can see how that belief has shaped a complete car, from the position of its driver to its exterior proportions and the engine we have chosen. The figures are exciting, of course, but they are only part of the story. We are building the One to make every moment behind the wheel more physical, instinctive and rewarding.”

Sanrivatti One price and availability

Prices and availability have yet to be announced, although having a completed show car is an important milestone for Sanrivatti. We can’t wait to see what the One looks like inside.

John Redfern writes for Motoring Research

Accountancy firm Saffery and one of its partners has been slapped with a near-£1m fine over its audit of disgraced Greensill Capital.

The Financial Reporting Council (FRC) imposed sanctions against Saffery and partner Michael Di Leto over the audit of Greensill Capital (UK) for the 2019 financial year after the firm and Di Leto admitted to 23 breaches of accountancy requirements, including professional scepticism.

The watchdog said on Monday the breaches were “serious and pervasive” throughout the firm’s 2019 audit of Greensill.

The supply chain finance firm collapsed into insolvency in March 2021 in the UK and Australia, with liabilities exceeding £1.6bn, resulting in a political scandal that linked the former Prime Minister David Cameron. In June, it was confirmed that Lex Greensill faced a nine-year ban from serving as a company director after he signed a legally binding disqualification just days before a scheduled High Court trial.

Despite the FRC finding the firm committed serious breaches of its regulations, it stated that it does not suggest such breaches caused the administration of Greensill Capital.

The notice stated that since then, Saffery have implemented changes and improvements to its audit processes and procedures generally, and Di Leto, who has worked since 2001 and served on the leadership board, has taken some remedial steps, “albeit the effectiveness of those steps have not yet been assessed.”

Saffery was issued with a financial sanction of £581,250, discounted from £750,000 for admissions and early disposal by 22.5 per cent, and Di Leto was issued a financial sanction of £124,000, discounted from £160,000 for admissions and early disposal by 22.5 per cent. Both were ordered to pay the costs of executive counsel’s investigation.

Simon Broadhurst, FRC deputy executive counsel, said: “This decision highlights the need for auditors to obtain a sufficient understanding of the audited entity and apply appropriate professional scepticism to information provided by management, as well as to consult on difficult and contentious matters as appropriate.”

“We acknowledge and regret that certain areas of the 2019 audit of Greensill Capital (UK) Limited fell short of the standards that we, and the market, expect. We are committed to the delivery of high-quality audits and take our responsibilities as auditors extremely seriously,” said Darren Drake, managing partner and Kenneth McDowell, national audit partner of Saffery, in a statement.

“As the Financial Reporting Council has noted, we have an ongoing programme of enhanced focus on audit quality, and we have drawn on lessons from the Greensill situation as we have strengthened our procedures, training, and guidance,” they added.

As the new Lord Mayor of the City of London, Alderman Bronek Masojada aims to unlock the UK’s economic potential by connecting talent, businesses, and investment across the country

I believe the UK is a land of opportunity.

That belief comes from personal experience. I arrived here from South Africa, built a career in insurance and found people who recognised my potential and gave me opportunities to succeed.

At Hiscox, we raised capital on the London Stock Exchange and grew the business tenfold, creating thousands of jobs, developing skills and generating wealth along the way.

My journey was not preordained. It depended on hard work, but also on people willing to open doors.

As I begin my year as Lord Mayor, I want to help create those same opportunities for others by connecting talent and capital to opportunity across the UK.

We have extraordinary strengths as a country. But too often, the connections between our talent, businesses and investment are missing. Addressing that challenge will be central to my year in office.

It starts with championing opportunity

We should be far more confident about what the UK has to offer.

We are home to more than 44,500 scale-ups employing 3.9m people, alongside more than 200 unicorns – the third-largest cohort globally.

We also have over £750bn of planned infrastructure investment over the next decade, spanning energy, transport, housing and regeneration.

These businesses and projects have enormous potential to create jobs and drive growth. The challenge is connecting them with the investment they need.

The City of London Corporation’s InvestConnect platform has already identified an initial £31bn pipeline of potential investment opportunities, with investors representing $3.8 trillion in assets under management signed up.

I intend to champion these opportunities at home and overseas, making the case for investment in the UK and helping connect investors with businesses and projects across the country.

But we also need to unlock more of our own capital for growth.

Here lies one of the great paradoxes of our economy. The UK has one of the world’s largest pools of domestic savings, yet growing businesses and infrastructure projects still struggle to access long-term investment.

International investors recognise the opportunity. In 2025, international pension funds invested approximately 16.5 times more in UK-managed private equity and venture capital funds than UK pension funds.

That raises an obvious question: what does international capital see in the UK that we sometimes fail to see ourselves?

The Mansion House Accord has established a clear direction, and the government is playing its part through the National Wealth Fund and British Business Bank.

But the private sector needs to move faster.

Employers should take greater interest in where their workplace pension contributions are invested. Trustees and investment managers should recognise the long-term opportunities available in UK businesses and infrastructure.

This isn’t about sacrificing returns for patriotism. UK-managed private equity and venture capital funds delivered annualised returns of 15.8 per cent over the decade to December 2025, compared with 8.4 per cent for the FTSE All-Share.

We need to create the conditions for more businesses to start, scale and stay in the UK.

And we cannot talk about opportunity without talking about talent.

Financial and professional services support 2.5m jobs across the UK, around two-thirds of them outside London.

Yet too many talented people still see the City as somewhere that isn’t for them. This is a perception I intend to challenge, building on the work of my predecessor, Dame Susan Langley.

I want to help more young people see what is possible, develop the skills and experience they need, and find genuine routes into employment and career progression. We will shortly be hearing more from the government on these shared aims too.

Through my involvement with the East End Community Foundation, I’ve seen how people living just minutes from the Square Mile can feel a world away from its opportunities.

That is something we need to change. Talent is everywhere, but access to opportunity is not.

The City has spent centuries connecting people, businesses and investment. It has the networks, expertise and international reach to make a real difference.

My aim over the next year is to put those strengths to work for more people, more businesses and more communities across the UK.

Because the opportunity is already there. Our job is to make the connections that help people and businesses realise it.

Of all the spirits clinking their way through airports, ferries and tax-free islands, one in three bottles will be whisky, much of it Scotch. While margins for distillers have always been tight, travel retail remains a great shop window for brands, as Ron Emler reports.

When the skies fell silent during the Covid-induced shutdowns of 2020 and 2021, passenger flights plummeted by 90 per cent, devastating the duty-free market.

Last year, airlines flew almost 10bn passengers, a near 7 per cent increase over the pre-pandemic level. The International Air Transport Association forecasts a further 3 per cent increase in 2026.

Duty-free spending lags behind the passenger recovery

However, passenger recovery and duty-free spending have not moved in step. Travellers are spending marginally less per head.

Consultancy Oliver Wyman calculates that last year, duty-free/travel-retail sales remained 0.2 per cent below the 2019 level, suggesting a $5bn revenue gap versus spending per passenger pre-Covid.

“We all had a tough year last year,” says Andrew Bardsley, Brand Director Prestige and Champagne at Pernod Ricard Global Travel Retail. “But we saw some volume growth [in Scotch].” He says there has been an upturn since July.

Scotch whisky leads growth in global travel retail

In 2025 overall whisk(e)y was the main growth driver in global travel retail (GTR), where it holds about a third of the spirits market. IWSR says that Scotch whisky sales grew by 10 per cent.

IWSR forecasts Scotch whisky has the major growth opportunity through to 2030 despite the fast-growing sales of agave-based spirits. Even allowing for travel disruptions via the Middle East, one industry estimate says that in the next three years Scotch could grow its GTR market by about $1bn.

The Scotch Whisky Association (SWA) says sales value through GTR outlets was £3.2bn in 2025, with blends accounting for £2bn and single malts for £1.2bn, though most of that will have gone to airport and ferry operators.

GTR gives distillers an additional route to consumers outside traditional retail and creates opportunities to grow sales around international passenger traffic and at the same time build brands.

The SWA’s Deputy International Director Emily Weaver Roads says GTR “provides valuable opportunities for consumers to interact with the Scotch whisky category, from established favourites to exploring new expressions and brands.”

“Whisky is one of the most sought-after purchases for Heathrow passengers,” adds Fraser Brown, the airport’s retail director. “With a bottle sold every 30 seconds, demand remains strong among travellers looking for a gift, a limited-edition bottle or a special memento of their trip.”

Ten seconds to win over travellers

“Travellers are a captive audience, but you have to capture them”, says Pernod’s Bardsley. “If we can get one extra percentage point of customers through the door, that’s a huge amount of money. But you have only 10 or 15 seconds to get their attention. Remember, our biggest competitor in airports is food and beverage.”

Barry Geoghean, the founder of brand consultancy, Duty Free Global, agrees: “If you’ve only got 10 seconds, you need to make those 10 seconds interesting. You need to have a point of difference, and you need to communicate that point of difference. But if you want to recruit young people, don’t patronise them.”

Diageo’s case for structural growth

Travel retail has the potential to deliver significantly greater growth than current industry forecasts suggest, according to Andrew Cowan, Diageo’s Global Travel MD, who believes brands and retailers must rethink how they engage with passengers and integrate into the travel experience.

“People shopping in duty free are becoming increasingly discerning, looking for unique experiences as well as products that are relevant to them and their journey,” he told delegates at the recent Cannes duty-free conference. “If you think about the current projections across the industry for low single-digit growth, you could convince yourself that that’s a reasonably accurate forecast.”

But he believes passenger numbers could grow by 6 per cent a year over the “next half century,” and says: “When passenger numbers grow by 6 per cent, we convert about a third of them into the category. So, we’ve got structural growth, a structural tailwind, a head start of 2 per cent before we even get out of bed.”

He claims just 11 per cent of passengers visit an alcohol duty-free fixture. Those who do purchase spirits spend an average of $85 per bottle – four times the average domestic purchase.

Pernod’s Bardsley is equally focused on making the duty-free experience special. “The need for consumers to find something different when they travel is incredibly important,” he says. “That’s why we have unique GTR offers and special finishes because of their exclusivity and where we add something unique to the liquid.”

Asked about the expense of those lavish airport displays, he admits: “The cost of taking prime space is huge and we have to weigh that up every year. But there is a bigger opportunity in GTR which is about brand building at the same time. Our job is not just to deliver commercially. Our job is to build brands.”

Significantly, Cowan says that 55 per cent of duty-free alcohol buyers purchase a product for the first time.

However, as Barry Geoghean points out: “Everybody can do price comparison. Now, there’s no hiding anymore. Consumers don’t buy on price; they buy on stories.”

So, for instance, a minimum price differential of 15 per cent is essential to sell into the US travel market.

Asia, Jeju and the new Scotch whisky hotspots

Where do they see the best bets for extra sales? “We have 8.5bn people in the world”, says Bardsley, “but only 1.15bn hold passports – 80 per cent of Americans don’t”.

Both Cowan and Bardsley are targeting Asia (where Bardsley says there is “low level” growth). India is particularly attractive, but China remains tough.

There, Geoghean says, you can only trade in the airports if you join the e-commerce operation. “But they have a list of 60m people who have bought Scotch whisky,” he says, so you gain entry to a potentially huge audience.

An even bigger structural change has taken place in the enormous South Korean market through the internal tax-free island resorts of Jeju. There, Koreans are allowed to buy two bottles of alcohol six times a year.

“A year ago, they changed the allowance from one bottle to a value of $400 to two bottles to a value of $400. There is nothing selling sub $50 anymore”, says Geoghean. “It’s all 15- to 21-year-old Scotch between $150 and $200 and they’re buying two bottles to take advantage of that allowance. That’s a dynamic which two years ago didn’t exist.”

Why cruises suit Scotch whisky brand building

He also points to the increasing importance of cruises, where passengers are not hurrying for flights or to get refreshments.

“It’s much more civilised. From a brand building point of view, a lot of what we’re doing with Scotch is masterclasses on board trips where people have time. They want to be entertained and it’s a better way to tell the brand story.”

The average two-year fixed mortgage rate stands at 5.51 per cent, marginally lower than last month’s 5.55 per cent but significantly higher than the 4.25 per cent before the Iran war, adding £200 to the typical cost of a new deal.

She said: “It’s understandable that some buyers are taking time to consider their options, and with budgets stretched, some may have even paused their plans for now.

“It’s unlikely we’ll see any significant fixed mortgage rate drops soon, so it’s key for buyers to decide on their priorities.”

Prices are falling despite buyers having the most choice in more than a decade, with the number of homes on the market at its highest since 2014. New-buyer demand is eight per cent lower than at this time last year and the number of sales agreed is down seven per cent. 

Housing market ‘depends on Washington’

This has put house prices 0.2 per cent lower than at this time last year, Rightmove said, putting the year on track to end with prices lower than in December 2025. 

Tom Bill, head of UK residential research at Knight Frank, said: “Buyers are working on tighter budgets due to the higher cost or borrowing, which has caused price growth to stall this year.

“With the conflict in the Middle East still unresolved, the outlook for the UK housing market next year appears to hinge on how events in Washington rather than Westminster unfold.”

Though house prices are falling nationally, London and the south of England have been worst affected by rising mortgage rates, as higher home values and stamp duty burdens weigh more heavily on buyers. 

House prices in the capital are set to recover at the slowest rate of any region in England, according to recent research by Savills, gaining only 8.1 per cent over the five years to 2031.

When a watch speaks to you, what voice does it have? Does it shout, all flashy, brash, and bold, or does it whisper, all refined, elegant, and minimalist, with just a touch of Bauhaus? Few minimalist watches answer that question as eloquently as the NOMOS Glashütte Metro.

When design and innovation speak for you, when your timepiece owns the office or bar, you don’t have to shout to get yourself heard. For over thirty-five years, NOMOS Glashütte has been quietly owning the city.

Born of a rebirth

Founded by Roland Schwertner in 1990, following the fall of the Berlin Wall, the company carries much of that Wiedergeburt, or rebirth, ethos with it. Watches have been made in the Saxon town of Glashütte since 1845, and NOMOS Glashütte continues that tradition of fine German watchmaking.

Surrounded by such watchmaking history, the company is rooted in tradition and is a member of Deutscher Werkbund, a German association of architects, designers and manufacturers, founded in 1907, that championed well-made, functional design and was an important forerunner of the Bauhaus.

When it comes to watch case design, the company also follows the principles of the Bauhaus: unadorned, straightforward lines based on geometric forms, with the focus on utility and quality.

A heart and soul of its own

Mechanically, NOMOS Glashütte is one of the few watch companies to produce its own escapement in-house (the assembly of the escape wheel, pallet fork, balance and balance spring that regulates the watch’s rate). In doing so, NOMOS Glashütte gives its watches a heart and soul that is entirely its own.

NOMOS Glashütte watches are almost entirely constructed on site and, since 2022, the special features of Glashütte watchmaking have even been protected by law, meaning the name “Glashütte” may only be added to a dial if at least 50 per cent of the value of its calibre was created in the town.

All 13 calibres, including both the automatic calibres and all hand-wound movements, are lovingly crafted in-house in Glashütte, and that passion shows in every minute detail.

From exquisite dress watches to bold pieces with cases crafted from precious metals that exude quiet luxury, by way of striking steel sports and stylish casual watches that all share the same minimalist DNA, they are all unmistakably products of the house of NOMOS Glashütte, identical in philosophy but very different.

NOMOS Glashütte Metro neomatik 41 Update: the city skyline in ice blue

Part of the Metro collection, designed by Berlin-based product designer Mark Braun and inspired by the many faces of the urban landscape, the NOMOS Glashütte Metro in ice blue mimics the ever-changing palette of the city skyline, with a dial that feels almost alive.

The electroplated and lacquered metallic dial dynamically shifts from a restrained cool light blue to almost white depending on how it catches the light, serving as a NOMOS Glashütte design manifesto for the wrist.

The layout follows on in the distinctive style of Mark Braun’s original Metro; again, hours are marked by dots and the minute track carries numerals at five-minute intervals, and it reads like a fine scale.

The elegant hands are slim and stepped in a shape reminiscent of the profile of the Empire State Building and sit under a domed sapphire crystal. A small seconds sub-dial sits in the lower half of the dial.

Despite its larger diameter of 40.5mm, the Metro neomatik 41 Update in ice blue looks fantastic and does not scream or shout on the wrist, while the ultra-thin automatic calibre DUW 6101 allows for a case thickness of just 9.1mm, which in terms of automatic watches is positively slimline.

On this version, the automatic Ref. 1166, the days of the month run around the outer ring of the dial face, with the current day framed by two teal markers. It is a beautiful use of the dial real estate that leaves the centre uncluttered, totally in keeping with NOMOS Glashütte’s design lexicon.

Metro date power reserve: a new hand-wound heart

But they’re not just pretty faces, since the Metro date power reserve, ref. 1121, is powered by the all-new hand-wound DUW 4701 calibre.

Flip the watch over, and the DUW 4701 is a source of wonderment. Visible through the sapphire glass exhibition caseback, the new calibre shows off Glashütte ribbing, perlage and temperature-blued screws, with a skeletonised balance cock that lets you watch the swing system at work. All of that in a thickness of just 2.8mm, with a 52-hour power reserve and a patented quick-set date.

With a case diameter of 37mm, it is no shrinking violet, or should I say teal; this version features that delightfully whimsical power reserve indicator. Rather than using a conventional hand to indicate the remaining running time of the watch, Mark Braun has gone for an optical portal where a tri-coloured indicator shifts from white towards teal as the reserve runs down.

Let your watch do the talking

While both watches are fruits of the same tree, they are the same, yet different, and sometimes, when it comes to being noticed, why not let your watch do the talking for you? Whichever NOMOS Glashütte Metro you choose, it will speak volumes without ever raising its voice. To see more watches like these up close, don’t miss City AM’s London Watch Week.

The Merseyside-based group said its GLP-1 ranges had helped it to grow its revenue by a half to £161.6m in the year to the end of July, lifting its pre-tax profit by 44 per cent to £40.6m.

Thomas Ryder, the former scaffolder who founded the business in 2014, said the group is entering its new financial year with “very strong momentum”. 

“Consumer demand for health, wellness and performance nutrition continues to grow and the market is moving quickly. We stay close to our customers, listen to what consumers want and move fast when we see an opportunity.”

Since it was founded little more than a decade ago, Applied Nutrition’s rapid rise has been buoyed by high-profile backers including Colleen Rooney, former JD Sports boss Peter Cowgil and petrol forecourt magnate Mohsin Issa.

Milo Bussell, an analyst at stock broker Cavendish, said the protein shake maker is “going from strength to strength”. The firm’s market backdrop is “highly supportive with consumers prioritising health and wellness and retailers expanding shelf space for the category,” he said.

Applied Nutrition has been one of London’s biggest success stories since its IPO in October 2024, with its shares up 133 per cent since its first day of trading. London’s stock exchange has suffered from a dearth of big-ticket listings in the two years since.

Ryder told City AM: “We’re honoured and privileged to be part of the LSE. We set out to be successful on the London Stock Exchange, and we have been, thankfully, and we just keep wanting to under-promise and over-deliver.

“As for the lack of other IPOs, I’m not too sure, if I’m totally honest, but what I can say is it’s been a great decision for us, for Applied Nutrition, and we encourage anybody else to take the same risk.”

    The West must stop accepting Russia’s narrative, and stop imagining that Vladimir Putin can somehow be assuaged or appeased, writes Eliot Wilson 

    When European leaders meet to discuss their ongoing support – military, financial and diplomatic – for Ukraine, there is often a kind of mad auction of rhetoric to see who can make the most solemn and heartfelt commitment.

    Sir Keir Starmer was a master of the art: “Our support for Ukraine is ironclad. We will stand with Ukraine for as long as it takes.” “Your fight is our fight, your security is our security, and the UK will not waver.” He was rewarded earlier in the year by appointment as the 92nd member of Ukraine’s Order of Liberty (though Boris Johnsona and Rishi Sunak are 75th and 76th). The usually inexpressive German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has said gravely, “If we in Germany waver, Europe wavers. And if Europe wavers, Ukraine wavers.”

    The President of the French Republic has not been outdone. Emmanuel Macron, whom Volodymyr Zelenskyy called “a real friend to Ukraine”, has said, “France remains unwavering in its commitment to Ukraine’s independence, sovereignty and territorial integrity… [and] will continue its political, financial, humanitarian and military support to Ukraine for as long as it takes.”

    The EU and nuclear weapons

    It would be wrong to suggest talk is cheap. The UK has committed £35.5bn in overall assistance to Ukraine, Germany has provided €30.8bn, France has contributed a more modest €7.9bn, and the European Union has made available €121.7bn through its central budget. These are not small amounts of money (though they have to be set in the context of the Trump administration ending any new assistance at the beginning of 2025).

    Yet sometimes politicians seem eager to embrace the White Queen’s challenge of thinking six impossible things before breakfast. As part of its desperately needed wholesale programme of rearmament worth €780bn over the next five years, Germany plans to strengthen its capabilities in terms of long-range missiles, or “deep precision strike” in the argot of warfighting folk.

    Germany and the UK are cooperating on a spectrum of these weapons, but the former will be responsible for the longer range variants, likely to include a hypersonic missile which can strike targets more than 1,200 miles away. It is not an unconnected observation that the distance from Berlin to Moscow is almost exactly 1,000 miles.

    This is causing the French government alarm: it wants Germany to set out clearly how it would use these long-range missiles in the event of a war with Russia. There is anxiety that a strike by Germany with a conventional weapon far inside the borders of Russia could provoke a response which escalated to the use of nuclear weapons.

    What this really means is that the French fear being held responsible. France is now, as we are perpetually reminded, the European Union’s only nuclear-armed member state, and President Macron has introduced the concept of dissuasion avancée, or “forward deterrence”. This would potentially see the deployment of elements of France’s Force de dissuasion, its nuclear-capable strike force, to other EU countries to provide them with additional security and reinforce the message of deterrence to Russia.

    France’s ‘nuclear grammar’

    One unnamed French official explained the problem to The Financial Times in splendidly lofty and patronising terms. As a nuclear-armed power for more than 60 years, France has a “nuclear grammar and vocabulary”, “unspoken” rules governing the threshold between nuclear and conventional weapons. This is, by definition, a theoretical issue for everyone except the Americans, who delivered the only two nuclear weapons ever used in combat. But French pride in their own sophistication is sufficiently robust to survive a nuclear exchange.

    “There are habits we developed over time. The Germans do not have it. It would be much better to have a clear and pretty public doctrine so that the Russians never get a signal wrong or misunderstand.”

    This is a challenging area. Germany agrees with the importance of “a joint doctrine and a joint understanding about the escalation ladder” from conventional to nuclear weapons. But the way the French have approached this – their “grammar and vocabulary”, you could say – runs the risk of allowing Russia to draw the West’s red lines for it. The framing of the conversation has provided the first draft of an explanation for any decision by Russia to cross the nuclear threshold.

    Within the first three years of his invasion of Ukraine, President Vladimir Putin had personally made 27 nuclear threats or threatening references to such weapons; collectively Russia’s leadership made 135 threats. On average, that is not far short of one each week. It seems both excessively delicate and rather too late to worry about provocation at this stage.

    Stop accepting Russia’s terms

    It is also fundamentally wrong-headed. Of course no-one should be reckless or irresponsible around nuclear weapons, but the West has not been; Russia has, repeatedly. The way France is approaching this is effectively to self-censor for fear of what might anger or provoke Russia, in the hypothetical scenario of being at war. Anyone in the Kremlin reading these media reports would instantly see the basis for a campaign of intimidation. It offers the framework of a way to curtail the West’s freedom of action and limit its capabilities without a shot being fired.

    Ultimately, this plays into Vladimir Putin’s hands, because it centres the notion of Russian victimhood. This has been his consistent defence throughout the war in Ukraine, that he has been forced on to the defensive by aggression on the part of Ukraine, NATO and the West. He is merely protecting Russia’s legitimate interests.

    It is sensible for Western powers to have a shared understanding, though perhaps one which is not wholly public or explicit, of how they would use their most potent and furthest reaching weapons in the event of war. Equally, the UK and France have long said, as openly as they can, that it would be unthinkable for them to use nuclear weapons as a first strike weapon. By contrast it was Russia which, two years ago, revised its nuclear doctrine and substantially lowered its threshold for using nuclear weapons.

    Stop accepting Russia’s narrative, and stop imagining that Vladimir Putin can somehow be assuaged or appeased. We know how expansive his ambitions are, and we have seen in the shattered homes of Mariupol and the torture chambers of Kherson how he means to fulfil them. The West should not – cannot – tiptoe around Russia if it came to a war. It is far too serious for that.

    Eliot Wilson is a writer and historian. He is a senior fellow for national security at the Coalition for Global Prosperity and a contributing editor at Defence on the Brink

    Ofcom has tightened its online safety rules, imposing new legal obligations on social media platforms and websites to detect illegal content, as Britain’s technology giants face mounting regulatory pressure.

    The watchdog announced on Sunday that platforms will be required to introduce more sophisticated automated detection tools, strengthen content moderation and ban users who generate or distribute child sexual abuse material (CSAM).

    The measures will extend the use of ‘hash matching’ technology, which identifies previously detected illegal material, to more services, including pornography websites.

    The largest social media platforms and file-sharing services will also be required to deploy automated tools to identify previously unknown abuse material.

    Subject to parliamentary approval, the new duties are expected to come into force in early 2027.

    The crackdown comes as Ofcom warned that existing safeguards were insufficient, with artificial intelligence accelerating the creation and spread of illegal content.

    “While we have seen some progress from industry on tackling child sexual abuse on their platforms, we are not satisfied that enough is being done,” said Oliver Griffiths, Ofcom’s online safety group director.

    “It is now for industry to step up, and any firm that doesn’t should expect to face serious consequences.”

    Tech firms face growing compliance burden

    The regulator is also tightening requirements around recommendation algorithms, forcing platforms to take additional precautions before suggesting content to children.

    Existing anti-grooming rules will be strengthened to ensure protections are enabled by default on children’s accounts.

    Ofcom also signalled plans to mandate specific automated technologies to detect other forms of illegal content, rather than allowing companies to assess whether such tools are necessary. A consultation on the proposals is expected by spring 2027.

    The measures add to growing compliance demands on technology giants including Meta, Tiktok and X under Britain’s Online Safety Act.

    The legislation allows Ofcom to impose fines of up to £18m or 10 per cent of qualifying global annual turnover, whichever is higher, for breaches.

    Earlier this month, the High Court rejected a legal challenge brought by Meta, Whatsapp, Tiktok and X against Ofcom’s demands for detailed information about their content moderation practices.

    The judgment strengthened the regulator’s ability to demand data from platforms, even before launching formal enforcement proceedings.

    The latest rules also come ahead of Britain’s planned social media ban for under-16s, expected to take effect next year.

    Ofcom said it would abandon some previously proposed restrictions on children livestreaming because platforms covered by the ban would instead be required to prevent younger users from accessing their services.
